In the updated analysis, the nonviral subgroup survival HR was 1.05 (95% CI 0.68–1.63). This imprecise exploratory estimate does not establish aetiology as a basis for withholding therapy.

The sponsor provided study drugs, collaborated with academic investigators on design, data collection, analysis and interpretation, and funded editorial assistance. Seven of 21 authors were sponsor employees. The report does not describe an independent replication of the analyses.
The article carries a notice that it was updated on 19 May 2020, five days after publication, without the content of the correction being stated in the text
32402160.n: IMbrave150 randomised 501 patients with locally advanced, metastatic or unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh A liver function, ECOG 0–1 and no prior systemic therapy to atezolizumab–bevacizumab (336) or sorafenib (165) at 111 sites in 17 countries. Overall 240/501 (48%) had HBV and 153/501 (31%) had nonviral disease.
32402160.bottom_line: IMbrave150 improved survival with atezolizumab–bevacizumab versus sorafenib (death HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.42–0.79). Survival at 12 months was 67.2% versus 54.6%, and median progression-free survival was 6.8 versus 4.3 months. At the first planned interim analysis, median follow-up was 8.6 months, 161 of 312 planned deaths had occurred, and median survival on combination therapy was not reached. Endoscopy and treatment of varices as needed were required. Dose reduction was permitted for sorafenib.
32402160.funding: F. Hoffmann-La Roche/Genentech funded the study, provided trial drugs and collaborated with the academic steering committee. Seven of the 21 authors were sponsor employees. The sponsor funded editorial assistance.

limitations: A national change in graft allocation policy and HCC priorities during accrual forced the trial to close at 45 of the planned 260 patients, which the authors state limits the strength of the conclusion
The authors state that predictability of downstaging success was beyond the scope of the study and would need specific protocols, particularly in hepatitis C
Explant pathology showed a tendency to tumour re-growth even after radiological complete response, which the authors report and attribute to the time to transplantation
critique: The report gives p=0.105 for interaction between downstaging response category and post-transplant survival benefit. This exploratory comparison did not demonstrate a difference between partial and complete responders.
Four controls remained free of progression. Two died of other causes and the other two had undergone ablation or resection. These counts cannot establish a modality-specific cure rate for TACE.

Centres selected the downstaging regimen and schedule. Two requirements were set in advance to improve comparability: selection by predicted post-transplant survival and sustained response before randomisation. Centre-level treatment variation limits comparisons of downstaging modalities.

The study randomised 45 of 260 planned patients and observed 21 deaths vs 87 planned. The corrected overall survival estimate favoured transplantation (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.11–0.92, p=0.035). Few events leave substantial uncertainty about the size of the benefit.

Two patients assigned to transplant declined it and died at 17 and 20 months. The article describes censoring at death but reports 5/23 transplant-arm deaths. Aggregate counts and Figure 2B do not establish how each individual event was coded. The published ITT estimate should be reported with this reporting ambiguity.

Survival is counted from randomisation, so the 29 of 74 enrolled patients (39 percent) who never reached randomisation, including 22 progressions and 2 deaths during downstaging, appear in no survival analysis; the trial reports no outcome for the downstaging strategy as a whole, which is the question a clinician faces at presentation

Controls were observed after response and offered further treatment at progression. The randomised comparison was transplantation vs this deferred-treatment strategy. The authors contextualise control survival against intermediate-stage locoregional treatment series. There was no randomised comparison with continued scheduled LRT or contemporary systemic therapy.

The transplant arm had higher residual tumour burden after downstaging (reported p=0.03). Two of 23 assigned transplant and none of 22 controls exceeded Milan criteria at randomisation. In a small trial, chance baseline imbalance adds uncertainty to the effect estimate.

Median tumour burden was 7.3 before downstaging and 0 at randomisation. Explant assessment gave 4.8 (IQR 3.3–6.7). The reported comparison (p=0.16) is compatible with regrowth during the wait, but the study did not establish that most recipients had again exceeded selection criteria.

Two of the 5 deaths in the transplant arm occurred within 30 days (myocardial infarction on day 10, multiorgan failure on day 20), a 30-day mortality of 2 of 21 transplanted patients, which is never stated as an operative mortality figure in a trial whose purpose is to justify consuming grafts

Eligibility required predicted 5-year post-transplant survival ≥50% using Metroticket, a model developed from retrospective data by a group including Mazzaferro, the XXL first author and chief investigator. XXL tested transplantation in this selected group. It did not independently validate that eligibility threshold.

Randomisation was stratified by sorafenib compliance during observation. Sorafenib was optional. Of 54 patients, 24 (44%) were not given it at clinician discretion or stopped it for intolerance or worsening liver function. The study did not randomise sorafenib or isolate its contribution to downstaging.

The primary endpoints were sequential: tumour event-free survival in phase 2b, then overall survival in phase 3. Tumour events included recurrence after transplantation or progression of residual disease in controls. The trial was open label.

A post hoc analysis estimated the 5-year survival gain using differences in restricted mean survival time. The publication describes subgroup gains of 26.5 months after partial response (95% CI 13.6–39.3) and 9.9 months after complete response (−5.5 to 25.3). The interaction p=0.105 does not establish different benefit by response or a listing priority rule.

A change in Italian allocation policy restricted accrual and forced early closure. The planned phase 2b/3 design included a futility rule. The monitoring committee recommended four additional years of follow-up. The small final sample limits precision. An efficacy-triggered stop was not reported.
Median donor age was 69 years (IQR 65–75), median D-MELD was 594, and eight of 21 grafts had ≥10% macrosteatosis. The trial did not estimate the effect of use of these grafts on other candidates.

Mazzaferro, the XXL first author and chief investigator, had co-authored the Italian allocation consensus and the tumour-risk models discussed. These links give context to the selection model. The investigators also reported individual financial disclosures.
32615109.n: 74 patients with HCC beyond Milan criteria and at least 50 percent predicted 5-year post-transplant survival on the Metroticket calculator enrolled at 9 Italian centres between March 2011 and March 2015; 54 (73 percent) were successfully downstaged and 45 randomised, 23 to transplantation (21 actually transplanted) and 22 to non-transplant therapy
32615109.bottom_line: XXL randomized 45 selected responders after downstaging, comparing transplantation with nontransplant treatment. Published five-year OS was 77.5% versus 31.2%, HR 0.32 (95% CI 0.11–0.92). Figure 2 on p. 953 shows both randomized outcomes. Early closure, selection before randomization and older comparators limit generalization.
32615109.funding: Funding and disclosures. The Italian Ministry of Health funded XXL (RF-INT-2006-394471) and reported no role in the study. Five authors (SB, MC, LB, SF and MI) disclosed industry personal fees or grants, including relationships with Bayer and BTG–Boston Scientific. The others reported no competing interests.

limitations: Small sample resulting from early stopping for efficacy at the planned interim analysis
Macroaggregated albumin scintigraphy was used as a surrogate for microsphere distribution
Generalisability to lesions smaller than 7 cm and to resin microspheres at 100 to 120 Gy is untested, which the authors state
critique: The trial was stopped at the planned interim analysis for efficacy and the survival difference is a secondary endpoint resting on 14 deaths in the personalised arm, so a 16-month median gain from 60 randomised patients is almost certainly an overestimate of the true effect

The primary endpoint was unmasked investigator-assessed response in one index lesion at three months. Masked central assessment also favoured personalised dosimetry (79% versus 43%, P = 0.0062), as did post hoc whole-liver response (14/28 versus 5/28). The progression-free survival HR was 0.71 (95% CI 0.39–1.30). Censoring at surgery, with 10 versus one resections, limits interpretation.

Ten of 28 patients in the personalised arm went on to curative resection against one in the standard arm, so part of the survival difference is surgery rather than radiation, and although the difference persisted after post hoc censoring at the date of surgery, that censoring was not prespecified

Eligibility selected heavily for a result: an index lesion of 7 cm or more, at least 30 percent hepatic reserve preserved, satisfactory mapping and randomisation only after the scintigraphy, so patients whose anatomy would not permit personalised dosing never entered

Safety was analysed by the actual dosimetry category assigned on central review. Eight patients randomised to standard dosimetry were reclassified as personalised, and one randomised to personalised dosimetry was reclassified as standard. The safety groups therefore differed from the randomised groups.

The 205 Gy tumour-dose target came from the same group’s earlier retrospective series (Garin 2012 and 2017). DOSISPHERE-01 tested a strategy using that target. It did not independently derive an optimal dose cutoff.

The control arm used 120 plus or minus 20 Gy to the perfused lobe, which the trial then shows to be inadequate, so the comparison is between a dose chosen to work and a dose the investigators already believed was too low
The device manufacturer funded the trial, validated the study design and paid for the editorial assistance, and the result supports its product's dosing approach
33166497.n: Sixty patients with unresectable HCC, an index lesion at least 7 cm, at least 30% reserved hepatic volume and no extrahepatic spread except hilar lymph nodes with lesions below 2 cm were randomised at four French centres to personalised (31) or standard (29) dosimetry. Fifty-six received Y-90. At baseline 53/60 (88%) had BCLC C disease and 41/60 (68%) had portal vein invasion.
33166497.bottom_line: In DOSISPHERE-01, targeting at least 205 Gy to the index tumour improved three-month investigator-assessed response versus standard lobar dosimetry (71% versus 36%), confirmed on blinded review (79% versus 43%). Median overall survival by assigned treatment was 26.6 versus 10.7 months. This small phase 2 trial stopped early for efficacy. Progression-free survival was inconclusive, and progression follow-up was censored at surgery in 10 personalised-arm versus one standard-arm resection.
33166497.funding: Funded by Biocompatibles UK, a Boston Scientific company and the maker of the TheraSphere glass microspheres used, which validated the study design and funded editorial assistance; the first author and most senior authors report grants or personal fees from the sponsor

limitations: Retrospective design, lack of a control arm and limited sample size compared with systemic therapy trials, all stated by the authors
critique: Sixty-four patients (39.5%) were classified as BCLC C because of ECOG 1 with cancer-related symptoms. The cohort had solitary tumours and excluded macrovascular invasion and extrahepatic disease.
The authors chose response and its duration as primary endpoints. Long survival and effective subsequent therapies complicate an overall survival comparison in early HCC.

Response depended on how it was measured. Localised mRECIST assessed the treated zone: 72.2% confirmed response vs 46.3% by RECIST 1.1. Best response using the same two definitions was 88.3% vs 63.0%.

The 3-year overall survival estimate of 86.6% includes 45 patients (28%) who later underwent transplantation or resection. Figure 5C plots a separate curve for the 117 treated with radioembolisation alone, without a numerical 3-year estimate or a comparison group.

The population is selected on every axis that favours the result: solitary tumour, Child-Pugh A only, no prior therapy, no vascular invasion, median diameter 2.7 cm and nearly two thirds under 3 cm, which is the size range in which thermal ablation is already curative

The 400 Gy threshold dose the paper proposes for an ablative effect comes from a subset dose-pathology correlation within this same uncontrolled cohort, so a dose threshold is derived and endorsed in the series that generated it

Two of the reported figures are internally impossible as printed, a median progression-free survival given as 57.9 percent with a confidence interval of 40.7 to 57.9 and a median overall survival given as reached at 57.9 with a confidence interval of not estimable to not estimable

The Discussion cites the 26.6- vs 10.7-month median survival comparison from DOSISPHERE-01, a separate randomised trial of personalised versus standard dosimetry in locally advanced HCC. These estimates do not describe the LEGACY cohort.

A single-arm retrospective series became the basis of a premarket approval, so the device's approved indication rests on a design that cannot compare it with ablation, resection or chemoembolisation in the same patients

The sponsor funded the study and supplied the statistical support, scientific input, trial management and medical writing, two authors are its employees holding stock, and the independent central review and auditing the paper offers as strengths were commissioned within that arrangement

Eighteen percent of patients were over 75 and 39.5 percent were labelled BCLC C on performance status alone, so the cohort mixes patients whose staging reflects symptoms rather than tumour extent with the very early tumours that drive the response rate
33739462.n: 162 consecutive patients with a solitary HCC of 8 cm or less and Child-Pugh A cirrhosis treated with Y-90 glass microspheres at three US centres between January 2014 and December 2017; median tumour diameter 2.7 cm with 62 percent under 3 cm, median absorbed dose 410 Gy, and 45 patients (28 percent) subsequently transplanted or resected
33739462.bottom_line: LEGACY supported FDA approval of TheraSphere for solitary unresectable HCC. In 162 patients, confirmed objective response by localised mRECIST was 72.2% (best response 88.3%). With RECIST 1.1, the corresponding figures were 46.3% and 63.0%. Eighty-nine of 117 confirmed localised mRECIST responders (76.1%) maintained response ≥6 months. Three-year overall survival was 86.6%. This retrospective single-arm cohort included 45 patients who subsequently received transplantation or resection.
33739462.funding: Funded by Boston Scientific, which also supplied statistical support, scientific input, trial management and medical writing; two authors are company employees holding stock and most other authors consult for the sponsor

limitations: Short post-transplant follow-up in a relatively small number of transplanted patients; the authors state it will take another 2 to 3 years to report the survival and recurrence data that would confirm efficacy
Three of the ten intended centres from two further UNOS regions could not supply data and were removed from the consortium, reducing power and applicability
The study was performed before the median-MELD-at-transplant-minus-3 allocation rule, so it cannot describe current waiting-list behaviour or access
Referral bias is possible because patients treated with locoregional therapy in the community who then progressed may never have been referred for transplantation
Centre-specific differences in the choice of first locoregional therapy persisted, ranging from 36 to 90 percent chemoembolisation across the 7 centres
Not all patients had AFP-L3, des-gamma-carboxyprothrombin or neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio measured at baseline, which the authors state limits the biomarker analysis
The authors concede that down-staging to within Milan criteria should be regarded as only a minimum requirement, given the under-staging rate
critique: The study population is conditional on transplant candidacy, not on tumour burden: 115 of 324 patients (35.5 percent) with eligible tumours were excluded for medical or psychosocial contraindications, decompensation with AFP above 1000 ng/mL, or bilirubin above 4, so the 83 percent success rate does not describe the patients a tumour board would consider for down-staging

Of 209 patients, 75 left the protocol: 51 for tumour progression, nine for liver-related death and 15 for other reasons. The competing-risk analysis counted progression or liver-related death as dropout and censored the other removals at delisting.

mRECIST response was assessed a median of 4.3 weeks after chemoembolisation but 6.3 weeks after Y-90 (p = 0.03), and radiation response is known to be delayed, so the central claim that the two treatments produced similar response compares measurements made at systematically different times

The chemoembolisation-versus-Y-90 comparison is non-randomised with large baseline imbalance (male 92.4 versus 72.6 percent, p < 0.001; multifocal disease 75.8 versus 51.6 percent, p = 0.003; MELD p = 0.04) and the choice was driven by centre (p = 0.001), yet every comparison is reported as an unadjusted p value and interpreted as no difference

Among explants with Y-90 vs TACE as first treatment, complete necrosis occurred in 4/13 vs 9/44 (p=0.76), and 3/13 vs 19/44 exceeded Milan criteria (p=0.44). These small comparisons did not establish a modality advantage.
First treatment was TACE in 132 patients and Y-90 in 62. The comparison of these two modalities covered 194/209 participants (92.8%). The other 15 received a different first treatment.

Tumour biopsy was not routine and nodules <1 cm did not count toward entry burden. Entry and downstaging were imaging-defined. Explant examination showed disease beyond Milan in 42.8% of transplant recipients.

AFP-L3 of 10 percent or more, the only independent dropout predictor, was measured in 83 of 209 patients (40 percent) and yields a sub-hazard ratio of 3.7 with a confidence interval from 1.27 to 10.79 from a model containing two covariates, selected from univariable screening at p < 0.1

Two centres contributed 68 and 33 patients (48.3% combined). Centre was examined in univariable analyses of understaging and necrosis. The modality comparison did not adjust for centre despite variation in treatment selection.

43.2 percent of the dropouts for tumour progression occurred during the mandatory 6-month wait before MELD exception points, so nearly half the progression events happened before the patient could be prioritised; the paper treats the waiting rule as biological selection rather than as an access barrier that the data could quantify

The 2-year cumulative incidence of dropout for progression or liver-related death was 37.3%. The crude all-cause removal proportion was 75/209 (35.9%) over the observed follow-up. These estimates have different endpoints and time bases.
Post-transplant survival of 100 percent at 1 year and 95 percent at 2 years falls to 83.1 percent by 3 years in the same 63 patients, and the abstract and lay summary quote only the 2-year figure

The study is presented as validating the UNOS policy, but the protocol being validated is the authors' own UCSF and Region 5 protocol that UNOS adopted, the validation was done by the same group at seven experienced high-volume centres, and the prognostic score used as the benchmark (RETREAT) is also the first author's
The first author reported serving on a Wako Diagnostics advisory board. Both the first and senior authors reported institutional research funding from Wako Diagnostics.
34331914.n: 209 consecutive patients meeting UNOS down-staging eligibility criteria at 7 US transplant centres in 4 UNOS regions, enrolled 2016 to 2019 from 324 with eligible tumour burden; 174 were successfully down-staged, 75 dropped out and 63 reached transplantation
34331914.bottom_line: The first prospective multiregional test of the UNOS down-staging protocol: 83 percent of 209 patients were down-staged to within Milan criteria, 2-year cumulative dropout was 37.3 percent, 46.6 percent reached transplantation by 3 years and 2-year post-transplant survival was 95 percent, with no detectable difference between chemoembolisation and Y-90. The finding that matters is the 42.8 percent of explants beyond Milan criteria, which shows that imaging-defined down-staging does not reliably identify the tumour it claims to; post-transplant follow-up was a median 1.7 years in 63 patients, and the TACE-versus-Y-90 comparison is unadjusted and confounded.
34331914.funding: Supported in part by a National Institutes of Health grant to the UCSF Liver Center (P30 DK026743); the first author reports advisory boards for and institutional research funding from Wako Diagnostics plus funding from Glycotest and Target PharmaSolutions, the senior author institutional funding from Wako Diagnostics, and two further authors multiple industry relationships

limitations: The systematic search closed in February 2020. ASTRO discusses later randomised evidence separately, including the Korean proton-versus-radiofrequency ablation trial and an abstract on EBRT after incomplete embolisation (NCT02323360).

For liver-confined HCC without macrovascular invasion, the search identified an interim randomised comparison of proton therapy versus TACE (two-year local control 88% versus 45%). It identified no published randomised comparison with thermal ablation by its cutoff. For intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, the panel separately emphasised limited randomised or directly comparative evidence and potential selection bias in observational studies.

The literature search was restricted to studies in which EBRT formed part of the treatment, so outcome data on non-EBRT liver-directed therapies were limited; a supplementary search of meta-analyses and systematic reviews was run but, by the task force's own account, heterogeneity in populations, tumour characteristics and outcome metrics meant it did not provide meaningful comparative data, and it was kept out of the evidence tables.

Supporting studies largely excluded Child-Pugh B8 or worse disease, and in the best prospective dose study 50% of Child-Pugh A patients progressed to a higher Child-Pugh class and 33% of Child-Pugh B patients to class C.

Technique, dose-constraint and motion-management recommendations combine evidence with expert opinion. Whether protons are better than photons is unresolved pending NRG GI-003 (NCT03186898), and the single-institution retrospective comparison that favoured protons is conceded to be insufficient to recommend one modality over another.

The task force states the guideline is not a substitute for multidisciplinary evaluation and discussion, and that future studies should further define the role of EBRT in the context of liver-directed and systemic therapies.
critique: ASTRO's own grading table permits a Strong recommendation at any quality of evidence, listed as 'usually high, moderate, or expert opinion', so the Strong first-line recommendation for EBRT carries no guarantee that randomised data lie behind it. A reader who treats 'strong recommendation' as a statement about evidence is being misled by the grading scheme rather than by the prose.

Consensus is assessed by a confidential modified Delphi on a five-point Likert scale with a threshold of 75% agreement, or 90% for expert-opinion recommendations, and recommendations failing the threshold are 'removed or revised'. No agreement percentage is printed for any recommendation in the document, so the reader cannot distinguish a unanimous recommendation from one that just cleared 75%, and cannot see what was dropped.

The Society of Interventional Radiology participated early and then withdrew as a collaborating society during development, a fact disclosed only in the acknowledgements. The withdrawn society is the one that delivers the TACE and TARE against which EBRT is being positioned, so the comparator specialty is absent from a guideline that recommends sequencing with and substituting for its treatments.

The ASTRO panel included radiation oncologists, a hepatologist, surgical and medical specialists, and medical physicists. The Society of Surgical Oncology and American Society of Transplant Surgeons endorsed the guideline. A later surgical perspective is identified from its citation and abstract.

ASTRO illustrates why resection, transplantation or ablation may be unsuitable, including comorbidity, poor liver reserve, tumours over 3 cm and locations affected by heat sink. Its first-line EBRT recommendation still requires multidisciplinary assessment of which curative options are feasible for the individual patient.

Cost, access and equipment availability appear nowhere; the word cost does not occur in the document. Recommendations that rest on proton therapy and on motion-managed ultrahypofractionated delivery presuppose technology concentrated in a few centres, and the guideline addresses a reader with neither only by saying the choice should reflect 'available technology'.

HCC and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma are handled in one document under shared key questions despite different natural history, systemic options and surgical pathways. The dose and constraint tables serve both diseases, and the bolded regimens in them are identified as the most common prescriptions 'based on consensus of the task force' rather than derived from dose-response data.

Hepatic toxicity is reported as change in Child-Pugh class rather than as decompensating events, hospital admissions or deaths, so the figures cited (50% of Child-Pugh A patients rising a class, 33% of Child-Pugh B patients reaching C) cannot be set against the complication rates reported for ablation or embolisation, and no numerical risk of radiation-induced liver disease is attached to any recommended regimen.

ASTRO’s conditional recommendation for postoperative EBRT in selected patients with resected intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma draws on two retrospective studies and low-quality evidence. SWOG S0809 offers indirect support for postoperative technique and fractionation. That single-arm study enrolled extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer and provides no intrahepatic disease outcomes.

Biologically effective dose is tabulated throughout on an assumed alpha-beta ratio of 10, applied unchanged across standard fractionation, moderate hypofractionation and ultrahypofractionation. The equivalence between the listed regimens depends entirely on that single assumed value and no sensitivity to it is shown.
34688956.bottom_line: ASTRO provides graded recommendations for external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) in HCC and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, with dose, fractionation and organ-at-risk guidance. It recommends EBRT as a first-line option for selected patients with liver-confined HCC who cannot receive curative therapy. At the February 2020 evidence cutoff, randomised evidence included an interim comparison of proton therapy with TACE. No randomised comparison with surgery or thermal ablation established which treatment to choose.
34688956.funding: ASTRO funded the guideline and states it received no commercial support. Members volunteered their time. The chair and four other members reported no disclosures. The vice chair disclosed Medtronic honoraria and consulting, and other members disclosed relationships with drug, imaging and radiotherapy companies.

limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede only that no portal pressure cut-off can be given for resection in the presence of clinically significant portal hypertension, that robust cut-offs are likewise lacking for the BCLC B subdivision, that the LEGACY cohort supporting radioembolisation for single nodules up to 8 cm awaits external validation, that there is no evidence base for sequencing after a first-line immunotherapy doublet, and, in general terms, that data for some encouraging interventions are still too immature to be incorporated into an evidence-based model and that observational studies have limitations for robust causal inference.
critique: This is an expert narrative review, not a systematically reviewed or GRADE-graded guideline. No search strategy, inclusion criteria, evidence tables or voting procedure are reported, so the reader cannot establish which literature was considered or how the recommendations in Figure 1 were reached.
Two authors drafted the first and final manuscript. The other 14 contributed critical reading and suggestions.

Figure 1 lists AFP, ALBI, Child-Pugh and MELD as refinements without a single staging rule based on these measures. Elsewhere BCLC discusses AFP thresholds for transplantation and ramucirumab (at least 400 ng/mL for ramucirumab), and bilirubin above 2 mg/dL or diuretic-requiring fluid retention as risks with TACE. These treatment-specific thresholds do not provide a universal staging cutoff.

Treatment stage migration allows a patient to receive another stage’s treatment when the preferred option is unsuitable. BCLC describes reasons to consider it and explains that universal criteria cannot be defined.

The radioembolisation recommendation for single nodules up to 8 cm rests on LEGACY, one retrospective single-arm cohort whose median tumour size was 2.6 cm. The upper bound of the recommendation is three times the median of the series that generated it, and nothing in the figure signals that the evidence thins across that range.

BCLC 2022 does not recommend resection for multinodular HCC within Milan criteria. It considers resection high risk in clinically significant portal hypertension but allows consideration of laparoscopic resection in mild cases, particularly for a single peripheral tumour with an adequate remnant. Surgical correspondence questioned other boundaries, including biliary tumour thrombus and the cause of impaired performance status. That exchange was available for this appraisal only through citations and abstracts.
BCLC 2022 discusses SBRT and calls for further prospective studies, although it omits SBRT from its treatment algorithm. BCLC 2026 includes EBRT among early-stage options in selected settings.

The figure is the product. Most readers will use Figure 1 alone and a figure cannot carry the qualifications the text attaches to it, so the caveats that make the recommendations defensible are separated from the thing that gets applied. The 2023 AASLD guidance reproduces this figure as its own Figure 9, carrying the algorithm into a second document without the text that qualifies it.

The evidence cut-off is 15 November 2021, so the document neither addresses adjuvant systemic therapy nor considers TACE combined with systemic therapy. It continued to be cited and reproduced as current for years, and nothing in it states an expiry or an update interval.

BCLC 2022 estimated median survival around three months for BCLC D. The 2026 update retains a median under three months for strictly defined BCLC D and uses under 12 months in Figure 5 for the broader group, which includes patients with longer survival.
34801630.bottom_line: BCLC 2022 links HCC stage, liver function, patient characteristics and treatment options. It includes radioembolisation for selected solitary tumours up to 8 cm. This expert review does not describe a systematic search or formal voting, and leaves several treatment and stage-migration decisions to multidisciplinary judgement. Two of the 16 authors drafted the manuscript.
34801630.funding: BCLC 2022 reported public and nonprofit research support, including Spanish, EASL, NIH and Horizon 2020 funding. It identified no commercial project funding. Among 16 authors, Reig disclosed relationships with nine companies and Bruix with more than 20. The article lists individual disclosures and institutional research funding.

limitations: The limitations of the parent trial apply, namely the open-label design and recruitment of patients with preserved liver function and reduced risk of variceal bleeding
This analysis was not powered for the subgroups, which the authors state
The authors note that the sorafenib arm performed better in median overall survival than in other first-line phase 3 trials
The authors attribute the increase in adverse events of special interest from 69 to 76 percent, driven by a 10 percent rise in immune-mediated hepatitis, to the longer duration of treatment
The authors acknowledge that the post-progression survival of patients who continued treatment would need a randomised discontinuation trial to interpret
critique: This is a descriptive post hoc analysis with no alpha allocated, so the p values are labelled descriptive in the abstract while the conclusion nonetheless states that the analysis confirms the combination as standard of care
Median overall survival of 19.2 months is reported from a median follow-up of 15.6 months, so the headline figure is estimated from the tail of the curve rather than observed

Exposure differed threefold between the arms (median 8.4 months of atezolizumab and 7.0 of bevacizumab against 2.8 months of sorafenib) and no dose modification was allowed for the combination against 37 percent of sorafenib patients having their dose modified, so the comparison is between a regimen patients stayed on and one they reduced

The claim about post-progression benefit rests on the 132 of 236 progressing patients who continued treatment and whose median survival was 24.1 months, a group defined by having survived to progression and been well enough to continue, which is guarantee-time bias the authors describe as suggestive

In the non-viral subgroup the hazard ratio for death is 1.05 (0.68 to 1.63) and the authors defend the regimen by pointing to preserved progression-free survival and response in that subgroup, which is precisely the argument that response and progression-free survival need not translate into survival

Immune-mediated hepatitis is reported in 53 percent of combination patients under a definition that includes diagnostic and laboratory abnormalities alone, which makes the number uninterpretable as clinical hepatitis and inflates the special-interest total to 76 percent

All five fatal upper gastrointestinal bleeds in the combination arm occurred in patients with macrovascular invasion (four Vp4, one Vp3) and only one was judged treatment-related, that judgment being made by unblinded local investigators with no central adjudication

Adverse events led to withdrawal of any component in 22 percent of combination patients and of both components in 10 percent, against 12 and 0 percent on sorafenib, so one combination patient in ten lost the whole regimen to toxicity

Nineteen percent of first responses in the combination arm occurred after week 24 and one at week 54, while all sorafenib responses had occurred by week 24, and assessments moved from 6-weekly to 9-weekly at week 54, so the response comparison depends on how long patients remained under surveillance

Twenty-six percent of sorafenib patients received subsequent immunotherapy against 3 percent of combination patients, which the authors correctly note works against the result, but it also means the trial cannot address the sequencing question clinicians face

The statistical analyses are credited to four sponsor-affiliated authors, medical writing was provided by a Roche-funded agency, and individual patient data are available only through the sponsor's own criteria on a request platform

The Discussion and Conclusion describe the longest median overall survival reported at that time in a first-line HCC phase 3 systemic trial. That is a historical cross-trial observation. Different populations and control-arm survival prevent a head-to-head ranking.
34902530.n: The same 501 randomised IMbrave150 patients (336 atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, 165 sorafenib) reanalysed at the 31 August 2020 cutoff after a median 15.6 months (range 0 to 28.6) of follow-up; 329 and 156 patients were safety-evaluable
34902530.bottom_line: A post hoc 12-month update of IMbrave150 giving median overall survival of 19.2 against 13.4 months (HR 0.66) and progression-free survival of 6.9 against 4.3 months, with an objective response rate of 30 percent and 8 percent complete responses. The p values are labelled descriptive because no alpha was allocated, the median survival exceeds the median follow-up, and the exploratory non-viral subgroup estimate was imprecise (HR for death 1.05, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.63), so it does not establish absence of benefit or justify aetiology-based exclusion.
34902530.funding: Funded by F. Hoffmann-La Roche/Genentech, which supplied the study drugs and collaborated with academic authors on design, data collection, analysis and interpretation; the statistical analyses are credited to four sponsor-affiliated authors, medical writing was Roche-funded, and all authors received support from Roche during the study

limitations: Open-label design with its risk of differential discontinuation, which the authors state
A cohort dominated by hepatitis B-related disease with very high intrahepatic burden, leaving the benefit unclear for alcohol- or hepatitis C-related disease
The authors state the need for a head-to-head comparison with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab
The authors say the 15-gene model needs validating in external populations
critique: The 15-gene predictor was developed in 54 patients and tested in 36 from the same trial, with a reported multivariable OR of 217 for the response classification. A small internal split can overestimate performance. Independent validation is needed for clinical use.

Downstaging and maintenance outcomes were comparisons within treatment groups. Median survival of 20.8 months among downstaged patients reflects selection after response and cannot quantify a causal benefit from downstaging. The 15-gene analysis was prespecified as exploratory and tested internally.

The trial was open label and reported responses of 31.5% versus 1.5%. In the sorafenib arm 19.4% stopped for toxicity. The two treatment strategies differed in adverse effects and delivery, which may affect treatment exposure. The available report does not establish the direction or size of assessment bias.

The authors themselves cite a meta-analysis showing sorafenib performs less well in hepatitis B-related disease, and 92.3 and 86.4 percent of the two arms were hepatitis B positive, so the measured difference is inflated by the choice of population

Catheter implantation was not technically possible in 2 of 130 patients because no main feeding artery could be found, which illustrates that the intervention depends on arterial anatomy that the trial does not characterise

In the high-risk subgroup the abstract and Figure 2A give median survival of 10.8 versus 5.7 months (HR 0.343, 95% CI 0.219–0.538), whereas the Discussion gives 10.8 versus 8.0 months (HR 0.470, 0.306–0.720). Table 1 gives whole-cohort macrovascular invasion in 185/262 (70.6%), the abstract gives 65.6% and the Discussion quotes the infusion-arm value of 72.3%. The 11.7 cm tumour median also applies to the infusion arm, versus 11.2 cm overall.
A single centre delivered every treatment in both arms, so neither the infusion technique nor the sorafenib management can be separated from local practice

The comparator was displaced by immunotherapy before the paper appeared, so a positive result against sorafenib leaves the clinically relevant comparison untested in exactly the high-burden patients the trial enrolled
34905388.n: FOHAIC-1 randomised 262 previously systemically untreated patients with advanced HCC and a dominant intrahepatic mass at one Chinese centre to hepatic arterial FOLFOX (130) or sorafenib (132). Overall 248 (95%) had BCLC C disease, 234 (89%) had HBV and median tumour diameter was 11.2 cm. Table 1 gives macrovascular invasion in 185/262 (70.6%), versus 65.6% in the abstract. The abstract reports Vp4 invasion or more than 50% liver involvement in 49.2%.
34905388.bottom_line: First-line hepatic arterial FOLFOX improved median overall survival versus sorafenib (13.9 versus 8.2 months, HR 0.408, 95% CI 0.301–0.552) and response (31.5% versus 1.5%). This was a single-centre trial in a population with large intrahepatic tumours (median 11.2 cm) and predominantly HBV-related disease (89%). It did not compare current immunotherapy combinations. The exploratory 15-gene model requires external validation.

limitations: Baveno VII notes that the workshop was held virtually. In NASH cirrhosis, clinical signs of portal hypertension can occur below an HVPG of 10 mmHg. A presinusoidal component can cause HVPG to underestimate portal hypertension in primary biliary cholangitis. The research agenda calls for validation of noninvasive tests across additional aetiologies and prospective assessment of HVPG versus noninvasive tests specifically before extrahepatic surgery.
critique: Baveno VII distinguishes manuscript disclosures from unrestricted workshop support and individual authors’ financial relationships. These are separate disclosures.

Baveno VII statement 1.18 identifies clinically significant portal hypertension as a risk factor for decompensation and death after HCC resection (A.1). It does not specify an HVPG or stiffness value that rules out resection.

The HVPG threshold of 10 mmHg is established for viral- and alcohol-related cirrhosis. Statement 1.12 notes that clinical signs can occur below 10 mmHg in a minority of patients with NASH cirrhosis (C.2).

The grey zone between the rule-out (liver stiffness 15 kPa or less with platelets 150 x 10^9/L or more) and the rule-in (25 kPa or more) is handled by ANTICIPATE at a 60% probability of clinically significant portal hypertension, as a weak B.2 recommendation. Sixty per cent is not a decision threshold for something as irreversible as declining resection, and the band it covers is wide: 20 to 25 kPa with platelets under 150, or 15 to 20 kPa with platelets under 110.

False-positive stiffness measurements occur. Baveno VII statement 2.11 advises repeating an initial transient-elastography result of at least 10 kPa under fasting conditions or supplementing it with an established serum fibrosis marker. It does not provide a patient-specific uncertainty interval around 15 or 25 kPa.

Evidence grades are assigned per statement but the studies behind them are not tabulated, and the document is 12,632 words of statements with the derivations left in the narrative. For the surgically decisive statements this means a reader cannot see how many patients, in which aetiologies, support a given kilopascal value.

Baveno VII identifies clinically significant portal hypertension as a surgical risk. BCLC 2022 permits laparoscopic resection in selected patients with mild portal hypertension and a suitably located tumour. In Yuan’s randomised superiority trial in HBV-related HCC within Milan criteria and with clinically significant portal hypertension, five-year survival was 69.5% after resection and 64.9% after ablation with or without preceding TACE (P = 0.325). The trial did not establish superiority or equivalence.

Patients starting atezolizumab plus bevacizumab are not covered. Bevacizumab carries a bleeding risk and these patients have portal hypertension by definition, yet no statement addresses variceal screening or prophylaxis before systemic therapy. A letter in the Journal of Hepatology made this point within months; that letter is identified here from its citation and title and was not obtained in full.

Pre-sinusoidal disease defeats the whole framework and is handled in a clause. Where HVPG underestimates portal pressure, as in primary biliary cholangitis, the reference standard and the non-invasive tests calibrated against it fail together, and the document says only that the thresholds are unestablished there.

Consensus is reported as statement-level evidence and strength grades with no agreement percentages and no record of which proposed statements failed, so, as in the later Baveno conferences, the published document shows only what survived the room.
The published text gives the noninvasive thresholds on pp. 961–963. Figure 1 on p. 963 summarizes the diagnostic approach.
35120736.bottom_line: Baveno VII defines clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) by an HVPG of at least 10 mmHg in viral- and alcohol-related cirrhosis. In compensated advanced chronic liver disease, liver stiffness at most 15 kPa with platelets at least 150 × 10⁹/L rules out CSPH. Stiffness at least 25 kPa rules it in for viral- or alcohol-related disease and non-obese NASH. ANTICIPATE estimates intermediate risk in those groups. CSPH increases risk after HCC resection, but the consensus gives no universal threshold for declining surgery.
35120736.funding: The participants reported no conflicts related to the Baveno VII manuscript. EASL, AASLD, eight national groups and three European research consortia supported the workshop with unrestricted grants. Two authors separately declared industry relationships, and foundation support was also reported.

limitations: Slow participant accrual required the eligibility criteria to be widened to non-surgical BCLC A disease, which the authors state
The trial did not apply the personalised dosimetry recommended by expert guidelines released in 2020, which the authors say may have limited the result
The authors call for a phase 3 trial to confirm the finding
critique: The planned interim analysis stopped enrolment for benefit after 72 of 136 planned patients. The small number of events makes the magnitude of both the time-to-progression and overall survival effects uncertain.

Five grade 5 events occurred with bead TACE and one after radioembolisation. Three TACE deaths were infection-related and classified as definitely treatment-related, including two with septic shock. The protocol permitted up to five sessions with up to 150 mg doxorubicin per session. The authors discuss this imbalance. Its contribution to the survival difference cannot be isolated.

The two arms treated different volumes of liver: radioembolisation was lobar or whole-liver in 26 of 33 patients (79 percent) while chemoembolisation was superselective in 29 of 36, so the comparison includes a difference in treated peritumoral parenchyma that the authors themselves identify as the probable mechanism of the local-control difference

Follow-up was unbalanced at a median of 28 months after radioembolisation against 15.6 months after chemoembolisation, and transplantation after downstaging was also unbalanced at 10 against 4 patients; censoring for transplant narrowed but did not remove the survival gap

TRACE used a single-centre, open-label design and assessed progression using mRECIST. The main report does not establish independent blinded central adjudication. Imaging-based comparisons should be interpreted in that context.

The safety population matches neither randomised arm, counting 33 radioembolisation patients (including one treated outside the trial) and 36 chemoembolisation patients (including two who crossed over after incompatible scintigraphy), so the safety and efficacy denominators differ and the crossovers move events between arms

Eligibility was broadened during accrual. Sixty-one of 72 patients had BCLC B disease, and about 70% had alcohol-related disease. In BCLC B, median time to progression was 12.8 vs 9.6 months (Y-90 vs bead TACE, HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.17–0.83, p=0.009). The report did not give separate OS for that subgroup.
This phase 2 superiority trial stopped at its prespecified interim analysis. The authors call for phase 3 confirmation.

Y-90 used a standard 120-Gy target for the treated volume. TRACE did not test personalised tumour dosimetry. The authors also discuss the excess grade 5 deaths in the bead TACE arm when interpreting the survival result.
35258371.n: 72 of 487 screened patients with BCLC B HCC, extended during the trial to non-surgical BCLC A disease and to ECOG 1 or Child-Pugh 7, allocated by minimisation at Ghent University Hospital between September 2011 and March 2018 to Y-90 glass microsphere radioembolisation (38) or doxorubicin drug-eluting bead chemoembolisation (34); 61 of 72 were BCLC B, 65 of 72 Child-Pugh A and about 70 percent had alcohol-related liver disease
35258371.bottom_line: In the single-centre phase 2 TRACE trial, median time to progression was 17.1 vs 9.5 months and median OS 30.2 vs 15.6 months with Y-90 vs drug-eluting bead TACE. The trial stopped at a planned interim analysis after 72 of 136 planned patients. The TACE protocol permitted five sessions of up to 150 mg doxorubicin. Three infection-related deaths in that arm included two with septic shock. Liver volumes treated also differed between arms.
35258371.funding: No funding source is identified and no author declared any relevant relationship

limitations: No masked independent reviewers and no comparison group, both stated by the authors
All procedures were done by interventional radiologists with more than 10 years of radioembolisation experience, which the authors note limits transferability
Inclusion criteria were strict, which the authors say limits generalisability to most patients diagnosed with HCC
Radioembolisation requires established nuclear medicine infrastructure and supportive reimbursement, which may not exist elsewhere
The explant pathology was not reviewed to a standardised protocol and the sample is only eight patients, which the authors state in the Discussion
The authors attribute the higher recorded adverse-event rate to the prospective design with extra visits and laboratory tests rather than to the treatment
critique: The sample size was set to detect a 30 percentage-point improvement in complete response over an assumed 50 percent with chemoembolisation, but no chemoembolisation arm exists and the 50 percent assumption carries no citation in the text, so the single-arm result is never formally tested against any goal and no p value or confidence interval against a performance threshold is reported
One independent board-certified radiologist with 18 years of experience assessed imaging response. The authors reported no masked independent review of the imaging endpoint.

Sustained complete response (90 percent, 26 of 29) exceeds the initial complete response (83 percent, 24 of 29) because partial responders converted later, and one of the 26 had only a single post-treatment image before being lost to follow-up, so the headline figure counts a patient with one assessment as a durable responder

Eight of 29 patients underwent transplant at a median of 341 days and five were lost to follow-up (13/29, 45%, combined). The 2-year cumulative incidence of target progression was 12%, treating transplant as a competing event.

The criterion for unfavourable location was a tumour within 5 mm of any of ten structures including the liver capsule, and 28 of 29 tumours were peripheral, so almost any subcapsular nodule qualifies; the premise that these were tumours where ablation underperforms is asserted from the literature rather than established for this cohort

Delivered dose was not standardised in any meaningful sense: the calculated segmental dose ranged from 181 to 3340 Gy against a stated goal of more than 205 Gy, and the PET-measured tumour dose from 190.8 to 3730 Gy, so the study cannot say what dose produced the response, and the 205 Gy threshold traces back to retrospective dosimetry series rather than to a prospectively validated cut-off

All eight explanted target lesions showed complete necrosis. Three livers also contained HCC elsewhere: an untreated 0.8-cm tumour, a 2.2-cm tumour previously treated by thermal ablation, and microscopic nodules with vascular invasion. Their time of onset relative to baseline was unknown. Median time to transplant was 341 days.

One patient with a solitary HCC of 3 cm or less progressed to advanced HCC with portal invasion and died at 296 days, attributed in the text to aggressive tumour biology rather than examined as a staging or selection failure in a cohort entered as very early to early stage

Grade 3 laboratory toxicity occurred in 17 percent, and the authors discount it on the grounds that all such patients had baseline abnormalities that CTCAE does not account for, without presenting a sensitivity analysis using change from baseline
Dosimetry was available for 26/29 patients (90%). Three exclusions for technical reasons represent 10%, although the article labels them 7%.

ClinicalTrials.gov first posted NCT03248375 on 14 August 2017, after the study began on 3 August 2016. The authors attribute the delay to an administrative transition. The public registration cannot establish the prespecified endpoint at enrolment.
The authors propose including radiation segmentectomy in the BCLC guidance. Their study was a single-arm series of 29 patients. The lead author advised the device manufacturer that funded the study.
35617978.n: Of 44 screened adults, 29 with a solitary treatment-naive HCC ≤3 cm in a location unsuitable for ablation received radiation segmentectomy at one centre. Two (7%) had a second planned treatment within 10 days. Twenty-four completed follow-up, eight underwent transplant and five were lost to follow-up.
35617978.bottom_line: In 29 patients, initial complete response of the target lesion was 83%, sustained complete response was 90%, and all eight explanted target lesions had complete necrosis. There was no comparator or masked independent image review. Thirteen of 29 (45%) underwent transplant or were lost during follow-up. Comparative recurrence and survival versus ablation remain uncertain.
35617978.funding: Funding and disclosures. Boston Scientific, the manufacturer of TheraSphere, provided an investigator-initiated grant and reported no role in conducting or reporting the study. The first author disclosed grants, consulting fees and a Boston Scientific advisory role. Four other authors disclosed industry relationships.

limitations: The target of 600 patients was not reached because accrual was slow, and the authors calculate that the conditional power of showing a difference had 570 patients been enrolled with a hazard ratio of 0.90 was under 8 percent

More than 90 percent of patients had a solitary tumour and about 65 percent a largest diameter under 2.0 cm, which the authors say may have influenced the result and means any advantage of surgery would be minimal
Successful ablation was not defined as the International Working Group's 5 to 10 mm ablative margin, which the authors list as a limitation
The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival rather than the time to recurrence that EASL recommends, although the authors argue this did not affect the result

The authors warn against extending the result to tumours in difficult locations, which were excluded, and to tumours larger than 2 cm, where diameter above 2 to 2.5 cm is a known risk factor for local recurrence

The sample size was estimated from the University of Tokyo's own retrospective cohort, in which the ablation patients had larger and more numerous tumours than the trial's, which the authors offer as the explanation for the better-than-expected control arm
Technical details of both surgery and ablation were left unspecified in the protocol and curability by surgery therefore varied across the 49 institutions, which the authors state
About 15 percent of patients in each arm were lost to follow-up after moving hospital
critique: Only 308 of 1,090 eligible patients were randomised because 778 declined, so the trial population is the 28 percent of patients genuinely indifferent between an operation and a needle, and two thirds of the accrual (197 of 308) came from 9 of the 49 centres with no centre-level analysis reported

The protocol explicitly accepted RECICL grade TE4b, complete response without an adequate ablative margin, as a successful ablation, which licenses the under-treatment that then shows up as doubled local recurrence; the paper lists the absence of a margin standard as a limitation without connecting it to its own success criterion

The Methods state that post-treatment complications were not collected, and the trial accordingly reports zero adverse events in 151 ablations and five in 150 resections with a median 17-day stay and 285 mL blood loss, so the safety comparison is uninformative in both directions rather than favourable to ablation

Histological confirmation was available in 131 of 150 surgical patients but only 30 of 151 ablation patients, with tumour differentiation unknown in 121 of 151 (80 percent) of the ablation arm, so one arm's diagnosis and grade were verified and the other's were not

The local recurrence comparison, 12 of 82 (15 percent) against 24 of 86 (28 percent), p = 0.07, is computed with ascertainment missing in 4 surgical and 1 ablation patient (and liver or extrahepatic recurrence missing in several more), with the greater missingness in the arm that looks better, and the counts in Table 3 do not sum to their stated denominators

The sample-size calculation required 285 per arm for a 10-percentage-point difference, inflated to a target of 300 per arm (600 total). A separate calculation of 123 per arm assumed a larger 15-point difference. These figures represent different assumptions.
Conditional power was <8% under an assumed recurrence-free survival HR of 0.90. This is a projection under that assumption. It cannot establish what the result would have been with full accrual.
The two co-primary endpoints are reported separately, recurrence-free survival here and overall survival years later, with no multiplicity adjustment described in this report

The surgical arm had better 3-year recurrence-free survival (54.6 versus 50.5 percent) but worse 5-year (42.7 versus 43.8 percent), so the curves cross; proportional hazards are described as confirmed but no test or diagnostic is reported

Fifteen percent of patients per arm were lost to follow-up after transferring hospital, yet the authors state outcomes were obtained with the support of the receiving hospitals, which is both unverifiable and inconsistent with counting those patients as lost

Of 308 registered patients, seven were excluded after registration. The modified intention-to-treat analysis therefore included 150 surgery and 151 ablation participants. Eight patients did not receive their assigned procedure. The 301-person analysis does not restore the seven exclusions.

The trial recorded Child-Pugh score and laboratory measures. It did not require indocyanine green retention, MELD or portal hypertension status. Outcomes by these measures of liver reserve cannot be assessed.
The Study Design section states the trial ran in 118 institutions while the abstract and Results give 49, a discrepancy the paper never reconciles
The authors disclosed journal editorial positions. The data availability statement provides access to data on reasonable request.
35949295.n: 308 of 1,090 eligible patients (28.3 percent) randomised at 49 of 118 participating Japanese institutions between April 2009 and August 2015, 197 of them from just 9 centres; 150 analysed in the surgery arm and 151 in the radiofrequency ablation arm, 90 percent with a solitary tumour and a median largest diameter of 1.8 cm
35949295.bottom_line: SURF compared resection with radiofrequency ablation for HCC ≤3 cm. Median recurrence-free survival was 3.46 vs 3.04 years (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.67–1.25, p=0.58). There were 301 analysable patients vs 600 planned. About 90% had a solitary lesion and about two-thirds had lesions ≤2 cm. Difficult ablation locations were excluded and the protocol allowed technical success without an adequate margin. The superiority trial did not establish equivalence.
35949295.funding: Supported by the Japanese Foundation for Multidisciplinary Treatment of Cancer and Health and Labour Sciences Research Grant for Clinical Cancer Research H21-015; numerous authors report lecture fees, research funding and advisory roles with Eisai, Bayer, MSD, Chugai and others, and four authors are the editor-in-chief, two associate editors and an editorial board member of the journal that published the trial

limitations: The sample was extracted from individual case reports and case series, so homogeneity may be compromised, as the authors state
The differential role of immunosuppressive regimens could not be assessed because precise data were missing from several reports
Comorbidity and the state of the graft, including advanced liver disease, were often not reported, so their effect on outcome and tolerance could not be assessed
Publication bias cannot be excluded because only cases of greatest impact are likely to have been written up
Response was defined broadly as disease control, and where imaging was not reported it rested on the original authors' clinical impression rather than RECIST 1.1

The authors state that PD-L1 staining should not be relied on as a predictive biomarker unless solid evidence is provided, and that no cut-off for a safe interval from transplantation could be identified
critique: The comparison of survival by rejection and by response is circular: rejection was fatal in 7 of 15 patients and 46.7 percent of those who rejected died within a month, so dividing survival by rejection status compares patients by their cause of death, and classifying a patient as a responder requires surviving long enough to be imaged, which is guarantee-time bias that the paper never addresses

Reported median overall survival and median follow-up were both six months (IQR 1.8–13.5). Eighteen of 52 recipients were alive at last observation and 34 died. Follow-up varied across case reports, limiting precision of survival estimates.
The estimated mean survival of 26.4 months in responders exceeds the 18-month horizon to which the restricted mean survival time was stated to be computed, and the paper does not reconcile the two

The Results report that all 4 patients with positive PD-L1 staining rejected and none of the 5 negative patients did, p = 0.008, while the Discussion states that the association did not reach significance; the paper contradicts itself about its most clinically quoted finding, which rests on nine biopsies in all

No risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of the 31 included publications is reported despite the stated PRISMA framework, and rejection was diagnosed histologically in some reports and clinically in others with the two pooled without sensitivity analysis

Attribution of 7 deaths to treatment as grade 5 events was made by the reviewers from published narratives, with no independent adjudication and no access to the primary records, in a setting where graft loss and tumour progression compete as causes of death

Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons is described in the Methods, but Tables 1 to 3 and the supplementary tables report dozens of raw p values across the same 52 patients with no indication that any correction was applied

The multivariable Cox model contains only two covariates, tumour type and interval from transplantation, and finds neither to be an independent predictor of survival, yet the paper's practical message, that an interval of about four years predicts response, rests on a single univariable ROC curve with 75 percent accuracy and a lower confidence bound of 61.4 percent

A published atezolizumab–bevacizumab case with a PD-L1-negative graft biopsy and no reported rejection over at least two cycles was excluded for incomplete clinical data. Its direction is consistent with the small graft PD-L1 observation. These case reports cannot validate a test for safe checkpoint-inhibitor use.
The review permitted reports of recipients of any age. The main report does not establish the number of paediatric recipients or permit age-specific estimates of rejection or response.

Non-English full texts were translated with Google Translate with queries resolved by native speakers, which is not a validated extraction method for the detailed immunosuppression and timing variables the analysis depends on
The corresponding author disclosed advisory-board roles for Eisai, MSD, Roche and AstraZeneca. The pooled case reports do not establish which checkpoint inhibitor is safest after transplantation.

The analysis addresses checkpoint inhibition given after transplantation, and the only interval examined is from transplantation to drug; the paper contains no data on a pre-transplant washout, and no interval of any kind predicted rejection, so it cannot be read as evidence about timing a graft after immunotherapy
36102312.n: 52 liver transplant recipients treated with an immune checkpoint inhibitor, pooled from 31 case reports and small series (median 1 patient per publication, range 1 to 8) published up to 10 January 2022; median age 62 years, 76.9 percent male, the original transplant indication HCC in 37 (71.3 percent)

Acute rejection occurred in 15/52 (28.8%) and seven died of graft loss (13.4% of all recipients). Disease control was reported in 23/52 (44.2%). These selected case reports lacked an untreated comparator. The hepatitis C and non-viral subgroups were too small for meaningful analysis, with only six HCV-positive patients, two of them also HBV-positive

critique: The one-sided p value for overall survival was 0.0180 against the prespecified boundary of 0.0193. The post hoc unstratified sensitivity analysis gave the same hazard ratio and a nominal p value of 0.0156.

The overall survival hazard ratio of 0.79 (0.63 to 0.99) is statistically indistinguishable from the 0.78 (0.61 to 1.00) that made the global KEYNOTE-240 trial negative, so the difference between a positive and a negative trial of the same drug in the same line is the alpha boundary rather than the effect, and the paper presents the similarity as corroboration

Progression-free survival and response were tested at the second interim analysis (30 June 2020 cutoff). Overall survival used the final analysis one year later. The abstract identifies the interim analysis in its Methods.

During enrolment, the factors for the stratified efficacy analyses changed from prior treatment, macrovascular invasion and aetiology to macrovascular invasion, alpha-fetoprotein and region. Small cells precluded a sensitivity analysis using the original factors.

Randomisation stratified patients by hepatitis B versus hepatitis C or noninfected aetiology. Of 93 patients without hepatitis B, only six had hepatitis C, limiting HCV-specific inference. Investigators recorded hepatitis status on the case-report forms.

After study treatment, 50.7% of pembrolizumab recipients and 66.7% of placebo recipients received systemic anticancer therapy. Subsequent PD-1/PD-L1 inhibition was also more frequent with placebo (28.1% vs 20.7%). The survival comparison includes these subsequent treatments.

Immune-mediated adverse events were adjudicated by sponsor review rather than by an independent committee, in a trial whose grade 5 treatment-related event rate was 1.0 percent against 0 percent on placebo

About 85% of participants came from mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan (about 80% from mainland China). About 80% had hepatitis B, median age was 54 years, all had Child-Pugh A liver function and over 90% had BCLC C disease. These features limit extrapolation to other populations.

Roughly 80 percent of patients were enrolled in a country where the drug was not approved for this indication at publication, so the trial established a benefit the trial population could not then obtain

The comparator is placebo plus best supportive care after sorafenib, so the trial says nothing about single-agent PD-1 blockade after a first-line immunotherapy combination, which is the only sequence now in question
36455168.n: 453 patients from mainland China, Hong Kong, South Korea, Malaysia and Taiwan with Child-Pugh A advanced HCC who had progressed on or were intolerant of sorafenib or oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, randomised 2:1 to pembrolizumab (300) or placebo (153); about 80 percent were hepatitis B positive, median age 54 years and over 90 percent BCLC stage C

critique: This is a guidance, not a guideline, and the distinction carries the whole weight of its grading. There is no mandatory systematic review, no GRADE and no meta-analysis, and Strong Recommendations are permitted at Oxford Level 5, which is expert opinion. A reader who takes a Strong Recommendation here to mean what a strong GRADE recommendation means elsewhere is reading one word for two different things.

Panel disagreement is reported exactly once, on coffee, as '12 of 15 agree'. Every other statement is printed with no vote count, so the only place the panel is known to have been divided is visible because someone chose to print it, and the reader cannot tell whether the transplant, TACE or systemic-therapy statements were unanimous.

AASLD’s 2023 adjuvant recommendation followed the initial IMbrave050 recurrence-free survival result, cited through a Roche announcement while overall survival was immature. AASLD reversed the recommendation in 2025 after the recurrence-free survival benefit was no longer evident.

AASLD statement 44 advises against combining systemic and transarterial therapy for BCLC B outside trials, citing negative studies of TACE plus multikinase inhibitors. Concerns about limited enrolment outside Asia addressed separate advanced-stage trials. Later phase 3 combinations improved progression-free survival in some settings. BCLC 2026 continues to reserve TACE-based combinations for trials.

Radiotherapy is handled thinly. External beam radiotherapy and radiation segmentectomy appear only as alternatives to thermal ablation in BCLC A, with no stage-specific recommendation for stereotactic body radiotherapy or proton therapy, and the document adopts the BCLC 2022 algorithm as its Figure 9, carrying forward the same omission radiation oncologists had already objected to in print.

Transplant sections are built around US allocation policy: UNOS downstaging criteria, median MELD at transplant minus three exception scoring, OPTN class 5 imaging. These are administrative rules rather than biology and change on a different timetable from the evidence, so the recommendations date quickly and transfer poorly outside the United States, and the document does not say so.

Surveillance is set by incidence thresholds in Table 1 while the text concedes that no risk score is accurate enough to recommend. The thresholds are therefore applied through aetiology and fibrosis stage alone, which is the practice the risk scores were built to improve on, and the circularity is not acknowledged.

Survival estimates for expanded transplant criteria come from different cohorts and follow-up periods. AASLD reports 75% at four years for total tumour volume and five-year estimates of 81% for UCSF, 71% for up-to-seven, 68% for extended Toronto and 65% for Kyoto. These figures do not rank the criteria.

AASLD Table 5 lists proposed indicators of unsuitability for TACE or Y-90. Examples for TACE include tumour burden beyond UNOS downstaging criteria and multinodular bilobar disease involving more than 50% of the liver. These are unvalidated indicators. Table 6 addresses treatment refractoriness. Neither AASLD nor BCLC 2026 establishes a universal tumour-burden threshold for withholding TACE.
The consolidated list prints the Oxford evidence level and recommendation strength beside each guidance statement. It gives no aggregate count by evidence level.
37199193.bottom_line: AASLD 2023 covers HCC surveillance, diagnosis, transplantation, downstaging, liver-directed treatment and systemic therapy. Its evidence levels and recommendation strengths are reported separately, and the guidance did not require systematic reviews for all questions. The 2025 critical update reversed the recommendation for adjuvant immunotherapy. Subsequent phase 3 trials have shown progression-free survival benefits for some TACE–systemic combinations. BCLC 2026 continues to advise against routine use outside trials.
37199193.funding: AASLD funded the guidance. Authors disclosed consulting, research funding, speaking, stock and other industry relationships individually. The first author reported consulting for multiple diagnostic, drug and device companies. The second, Llovet, listed consulting relationships with 13 companies.

Relatively short follow-up at this interim analysis, although 33 and 40 percent of patients had already recurred or died

critique: The trial was declared positive with no estimable median recurrence-free survival in either arm, the entire result resting on a hazard ratio whose adjusted upper bound of 0.98 nearly touches 1 against a design whose minimum detectable difference was 0.8

The statistical analysis plan specified that a positive interim analysis would make the final analysis at 323 events descriptive only, so the design guarantees that the mature estimate can never be formally tested; the subsequent update showed the hazard ratio drifting to 0.90

Investigators could offer crossover at recurrence and could resect or ablate a recurrence first. Overall survival therefore reflects an initial treatment strategy followed by subsequent care. Crossover complicates attribution of survival to the adjuvant drug alone.

Patients in the surveillance arm more often had a tumour larger than 5 cm (175 of 292, 60 percent, against 152 of 293, 52 percent), an eight-point imbalance in the strongest prognostic factor in a trial whose headline hazard ratio is 0.72

The high-risk criteria are tumour-morphology based and partly require a resection specimen (microvascular invasion, differentiation grade), so the 83 ablation patients were selected by size and number alone and belong to a different risk construct than the 585 resected patients

The subgroup pattern runs against the enrolment: the hazard ratio was 0.61 (0.38 to 0.97) in the rest of the world against 0.80 (0.59 to 1.08) in Asia-Pacific excluding Japan where 71 percent of patients were recruited, and 1.13 (0.67 to 1.91) in ECOG 1 patients, with the figure legend stating that none of these confidence intervals is adjusted for multiplicity

A single post-resection TACE was permitted before randomisation, received by 11–12% of resected patients, and included as a stratification factor. This subgroup’s recurrence-free survival HR was 1.21 (95% CI 0.57–2.59). The wide interval limits interpretation of differential benefit.

Grade 5 adverse events occurred in six atezolizumab-bevacizumab patients (2 percent), two of them treatment-related, against one in the surveillance arm, in a population rendered disease-free by curative-intent surgery and most of whom would not have recurred within the treatment year

Figure 3 reports recurrence-free survival by tumour PD-L1 expression. HRs were 0.82 (95% CI 0.55–1.20) for expression at least 1% and 0.62 (0.43–0.91) for expression below 1%. These exploratory subgroup estimates do not establish that PD-L1 predicts adjuvant benefit.

Among 914 patients assessed, screening excluded 57 with residual, recurrent or metastatic disease and 26 without signed consent. If independent review later identified disease already present at baseline, the trial counted recurrence at randomisation.

The sponsor collaborated with the academic steering committee on design, data collection, analysis and interpretation. Sponsor statistician QL conducted the analyses. QL and academic investigator PKHC both verified the underlying data.

The Discussion proposes that the results could lead to new considerations in the clinical indications for surgical resection, an inference about operative decision-making drawn from a surrogate endpoint at an interim analysis
