The trial was neither designed nor powered to compare STRIDE with durvalumab monotherapy, which the authors state
critique: The authors report delayed separation of the survival curves and exploratory analyses by time interval. The formal exploratory treatment-by-time interaction tests were nonsignificant for both immunotherapy comparisons.

Before nine months, the overall survival HR versus sorafenib was 0.87 (95% CI 0.68–1.11) for STRIDE and 0.98 (0.77–1.24) for durvalumab. The later STRIDE estimate was 0.70. The exploratory interaction tests were nonsignificant. These intervals do not identify a time before which individuals cannot benefit.

Median overall survival was 16.56 months with durvalumab alone and 16.43 months with STRIDE. Survival at three years was 24.7% and 30.7%, respectively. The trial did not formally compare the two immunotherapy arms and cannot isolate the incremental effect of tremelimumab.

The non-inferiority margin for durvalumab against sorafenib was an upper bound of 1.08 and the observed bound was 1.03, so the claim rests on clearing a tight margin whose derivation is not shown in the paper

The final analysis was performed at 47 months with 555 events in the STRIDE and sorafenib arms against a plan of 515 events at about 37.5 months, and the paper does not explain the 10-month delay or the extra events

Progression-free survival did not differ significantly among the three arms and response, time to progression and duration of response were all investigator-assessed with no blinded independent central review, in a fully open-label trial

Treatment beyond progression was markedly asymmetric (46.9 percent of STRIDE and 48.5 percent of durvalumab patients against 35.8 percent on sorafenib) and 30 STRIDE patients were retreated with tremelimumab, so the arms differ in exposure and in post-progression management in a way an open-label design cannot separate from the drug effect

The T75 plus durvalumab arm was closed on the basis of a preplanned analysis of the still-running supporting phase 2 trial, so a design change in the phase 3 trial was driven by interim data from another study, and the 155 patients already randomised to it have no efficacy result reported at all

Only 40.7 to 45.0 percent of patients received any second-line therapy after discontinuation, so overall survival is largely the natural history of untreated progression and the trial says nothing about sequencing

Grade 3 or 4 treatment-emergent adverse events were 50.5 percent with STRIDE against 52.4 percent with sorafenib, so the regimen is differently toxic rather than less toxic, an observation the abstract reports numerically without making

Histological confirmation and a fresh or recent biopsy were required, which selects a biopsy-willing and biopsy-feasible population unrepresentative of HCC practice, and PD-L1 status was still missing in 11 to 13 percent of patients

The baseline table includes small numbers with Child-Pugh B7 (1.0–2.6% by arm), ECOG 2 (0.3–0.5%) and three classified as Child-Pugh “other”, although the planned population was Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0–1. These groups cannot support separate efficacy estimates.

Median time to deterioration of patient-reported global health status was 7.5 months with STRIDE, 7.4 with durvalumab and 5.7 with sorafenib. HRs versus sorafenib were 0.76 (95% CI 0.61–0.96) and 0.77 (0.62–0.96). Participants knew their assigned treatment, which can influence self-reported outcomes.

The sponsor provided the drugs and collaborated on design, collection, analysis and interpretation, six authors are its employees, and the authors and sponsor jointly vouch for the data, so no analysis independent of AstraZeneca underlies the result

limitations: Small sample and short post-procedure follow-up, which the authors attribute to the study design
The technical-success performance goal, although literature-based, was agreed with the FDA on the basis of achievable enrolment and was not intended to identify a difference from existing therapies
The 30-day efficacy assessment was extrapolated from thermal-ablation response standards despite histotripsy's different mechanism, with no validated treatment-response criteria available
The investigators found procedure time difficult to compare with other therapies because they had no prior experience with this externally delivered treatment.

The population was not typical of patients who undergo ablative therapy because many had stage IV metastatic disease, which the authors say limits comparison with established local-regional treatments
The authors acknowledge the grade 5 complication and note that although the participant met the hepatic-function entry criteria their underlying liver function was likely tenuous
critique: The technical-success denominator was reduced from 49 treated tumours to 44 by excluding five tumours with poor image quality or no contrast, and the protocol states that only participants with complete imaging data entered the technical-success cohort, so the lesions in which coverage could not be confirmed were removed from the measure of whether coverage was achieved
The 70% technical-success target lies near the middle of the published 48–95% range the authors cite for thermal ablation. Meeting this single-arm target does not establish comparative performance.

The primary effectiveness endpoint was target coverage on imaging within 36 hours. At 30 days, technique efficacy was 30/36 evaluable lesions (83%). Six lacked follow-up imaging and two scans were unreadable. The endpoints and denominators differ, so these percentages do not quantify progression between the two assessments.

The 30-day technique efficacy differed starkly by geography, 14 of 20 (70 percent) at United States sites versus 16 of 16 (100 percent) in Europe, a difference visible in Table 2 that is not reported in the text or examined

Treated tumours averaged 1.5 cm and sat in segments II, III, IVa, IVb, V and VI, with 24 of 44 in segment III and none in segments VII or VIII; treatment depth was not even recorded, so feasibility in the deep, dome and subdiaphragmatic locations where percutaneous ablation is hardest is untested

The mean imaging treatment zone was 3.6 cm in diameter and 17.5 cm³, versus 1.5 cm and 1.6 cm³ for the mean target lesion. A treatment margin includes surrounding liver. These imaging volumes do not quantify loss of functional liver tissue.

One participant developed grade 5 hepatic failure on day 12 and died on day 37. The report counted the event within the 30-day safety period and recorded no death within 30 days. The report does not establish whether mistargeting or inadequate treatment volume contributed to this event.

Table 1 reports baseline lesion counts in bands. Four of 25 participants with metastatic disease and an available count had more than 20 liver lesions, and one participant with HCC had 11–15. Technical success in the treated target does not measure control of untreated disease.

The authors cite published ranges from 12 references for ablation outcomes and describe comparisons across studies as difficult. Without matched populations or common outcome definitions, the observed 95% technical success and 7% major complication rate do not establish comparative safety or efficacy.

limitations: EASL limits the update to selected questions and refers to its 2018 guideline elsewhere. It finds insufficient evidence to prefer resection or locoregional therapy for cirrhotic patients with multiple resectable tumours, to recommend HCC surveillance for advanced fibrosis without cirrhosis, or to use prognostic scores alone for treatment selection. It discourages unrestricted systemic treatment in Child-Pugh B but permits consideration in carefully selected patients with scores 7–8 (level 3, weak). Trials generally excluded post-transplant recurrence.
critique: All recommendations passed the Delphi process. Two items had 75% agreement, one on bland embolisation and one on gadoxetic acid MRI before curative treatment. Both are labelled consensus even though 75% falls within the stated 50–75% majority-agreement band. The printed percentage helps distinguish these from near-unanimous votes.

EASL incorporated meeting abstracts when full trial results were unavailable. Abstracts can omit details needed to assess design, conduct and analysis. Evidence based on an abstract should be reassessed against the full report when available.

No disclosures are printed. The conflict-of-interest section is a single pointer to ICMJE forms held elsewhere, so a reader weighing the panel's positions on SIRT, on checkpoint inhibitors or on drug-eluting beads cannot see who is paid by the manufacturers. Both the 2022 BCLC update and the 2023 AASLD guidance print theirs in full.

EASL regards AFP above 1,000 ng/mL as a contraindication to transplantation and requires AFP at or below 1,000 for at least three months before listing patients downstaged to Milan criteria. In the United States, OPTN Policy 9.5.I.iv governs standard HCC exception priority. If AFP ever exceeded 1,000, a candidate who otherwise qualifies must have AFP below 500 after locoregional therapy and maintain it below 500. Cases outside the standard rule require individual review for exception priority. Transplant candidacy is a separate centre decision.

EASL recommends against resection solely to downstage disease beyond Milan criteria for transplant eligibility (level 4, 83% agreement). Two surgical items drew lower agreement at 80%. This recommendation concerns deliberate surgical downstaging. It does not address every patient considered for salvage transplantation after recurrence following curative-intent resection.

For portal vein invasion, EASL recommends against substituting radioembolisation for systemic therapy (level 3, strong, 86% agreement). SARAH and SIRveNIB directly compared radioembolisation with sorafenib. DOSISPHERE-01 instead compared two radioembolisation dosimetry strategies and improved response (71% versus 36%). EASL also quotes survival by achieved tumour dose and calls for a randomised comparison of contemporary radioembolisation with systemic therapy.

EASL cites two meta-analyses in supporting the use of either radiofrequency or microwave ablation (level 2). BCLC 2026 favours microwave ablation for local control in selected tumours up to about 3–4 cm. The statements address different questions. Neither establishes a general survival advantage of one thermal technique.

Levels of evidence are assigned per recommendation without a table showing the number and design of studies behind each, so the reader must follow the narrative and its reference numbers. For the recommendations that decide a surgical case, resection for single HCC above 2 cm at LoE 2 and the minimally invasive approach where feasible, that narrative rests on observational series and propensity analyses whose selection bias the document acknowledges elsewhere but not there.

The guideline is explicitly partial and says so once, in a paragraph next to the corresponding-author footnote. There is no list of what is and is not covered, so a reader cannot tell which parts of a sixty-page document are current and which have been left to the 2018 guideline by silence.

In the extracted text the inequality signs are repeatedly mangled, so the thresholds that decide eligibility read as 'solitary HCC <-2 cm', '<-3 tumours' and '<-6.5 cm'. Every size and AFP cut-off in this copy must be checked against the published typesetting before it is used.

Examples include an AFP listing threshold, no general preference between radiofrequency and microwave ablation, and a recommendation against using resection to downstage beyond-Milan disease for transplant eligibility. The update covers selected clinical questions and refers to the 2018 guideline elsewhere. Many surgical and transplant recommendations rely on nonrandomised cohorts, case-control studies or case series (levels 3–4).

critique: The primary endpoint is a composite counting death from any cause and the arms reached it differently: 8 of 14 radiotherapy events were deaths without local progression against 7 of 27 for ablation, so the significant result rests on a difference of about 14 local progression events in 166 patients

Local progression was defined within 1 cm of the ablation zone or the radiation target volume, as applicable. Imaging readers were blinded to patient outcomes. Both local progression-free survival and 3-year local control favoured SBRT (3-year local control 92.8% vs 75.9%, reported OR for local failure 0.25, 95% CI 0.09–0.65, p=0.005).

Three ablation patients needed a second session to achieve complete ablation and were not counted as local failures, a convention that moves early technical failures out of the endpoint in the arm that lost on it

The population is a best case for both modalities: single centre, 88 percent hepatitis B, over 90 percent Child-Pugh 5, median tumour 1.6 to 1.7 cm with about 70 percent at 2 cm or less, so the result applies to the easiest recurrences rather than to the perivascular or subcapsular ones where the choice is hard

Both arms were delivered by one group at one high-volume centre, with a guaranteed ablation margin over 1 cm that most units would not reliably achieve, so the control arm is also a best case
Open-label with no central imaging review, acknowledged by the authors, in a trial whose entire positive result is an imaging judgment

The grade ≥3 treatment-related event totals were 37/88 with sorafenib and 39/83 with SBRT plus sorafenib (42% vs 47%, p=0.52). The grade 3, 4 and 5 counts in the Results sum to these totals (30+5+2 and 35+3+1). The report does not tabulate each patient’s worst grade.

Radiotherapy dose was personalised from 27.5 to nearly twofold higher at 50 Gy in 5 fractions according to liver tolerance, so the experimental arm is a range of treatments rather than one, and no dose-response analysis is presented
39699905.n: 193 patients randomised and 177 eligible and analysed at 23 sites in the USA, Canada, Australia and Hong Kong between April 2013 and March 2021: 92 to sorafenib alone and 85 to personalised stereotactic body radiotherapy of 27.5 to 50 Gy in 5 fractions followed by sorafenib; 145 of 177 were BCLC C, macrovascular invasion was present in 131 (74.0 percent) and 112 (63.3 percent) had Vp3, Vp4 or inferior vena cava involvement
39699905.bottom_line: NRG/RTOG 1112 compared SBRT followed by sorafenib with sorafenib alone in locally advanced HCC. Median overall survival was 15.8 vs 12.3 months. The prespecified unadjusted primary test missed its boundary (one-sided p=0.06), while the adjusted model estimated a 28% lower death hazard. Early closure reduced power to 65% with 177 eligible patients vs 368 planned. The trial did not compare SBRT added to first-line immunotherapy.
39699905.funding: Funded by National Cancer Institute grants U10CA180868, U10CA180822, UG1CA189867 and U24CA180803; the funder had no role in design, conduct, analysis or the decision to publish, although several authors report industry payments outside the submitted work

limitations: Overall survival was immature at this first interim analysis and did not cross its boundary, which the authors state

The planned sample size was reduced from 950 to 450 because of slow accrual during the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving about 79 percent power for the overall survival hazard ratio of 0.73 even at the final analysis
critique: The protocol permitted TACE and excluded radioembolisation. The trial therefore provides a comparison for TACE-based treatment only.

The progression assessment allowed up to five target liver lesions, required LI-RADS 5 for new intrahepatic tumours and deferred assessment until the first 9-week scan and treatment of all target tumours. Removing the LI-RADS 5 requirement left median PFS at 14.6 months with combination therapy and reduced the control median from 10.0 to 8.4 months (sensitivity HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.49–0.80, vs primary HR 0.66). The requirement narrowed the observed difference.

The trial is positive on a progression endpoint of its own construction while overall survival, the dual primary endpoint, missed its boundary at a hazard ratio of 0.80 whose confidence interval crosses 1, so nothing yet shows that patients live longer

Nearly a third of participants were BCLC stage A and a further 10 percent stage C, so fewer than 60 percent had the intermediate-stage disease for which chemoembolisation is indicated, and the stage A patients were exposed to the full toxicity of a doublet systemic regimen

Grade ≥3 treatment-related events occurred in 71% with the combination and 32% with control. Immune-mediated events occurred in 48% with the combination and four treatment-related deaths included hepatic failure and immune-mediated hepatitis. Nearly one-third had BCLC A disease, but eligibility required liver-confined disease unsuitable for curative treatment.

Chemoembolisation technique was prespecified by site and could be conventional or drug-eluting bead, with split procedures allowed and a maximum of two treatments per tumour, so the control intervention is heterogeneous across 137 sites and its quality cannot be audited from the report

Seventy-two percent of participants were Asian. Hepatitis B markers were present in 62% (including core-antibody positivity alone), alcohol was recorded as an aetiology in 46% and nonviral disease in 27%. Aetiologies could overlap.
Patient-reported outcomes and quality of life are not reported, which is what would justify a progression-free survival endpoint at these rates of toxicity

The result is the first of four planned interim analyses, final for progression-free survival only, so the trial's own structure means the progression endpoint can no longer be tested while survival testing continues
The funders reported a role in study design, data collection, data analysis, interpretation and writing the report.

There is no arm receiving systemic therapy without chemoembolisation, so the question a tumour board faces for a patient with high tumour burden, whether to add chemoembolisation to systemic therapy rather than the reverse, is untouched
39798578.n: 480 of 847 screened patients with liver-confined unresectable HCC amenable to chemoembolisation, Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0 to 1, randomised 1:1 at 137 sites in 33 countries between May 2020 and January 2023 to lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab plus TACE (237) or dual placebo plus TACE (243); by BCLC stage 148 were A, 281 B and 50 C, and 72 percent were Asian
39798578.bottom_line: In liver-confined HCC unsuitable for curative treatment, adding lenvatinib and pembrolizumab to TACE prolonged median progression-free survival from 10.0 to 14.6 months (HR 0.66). Removing the trial-specific LI-RADS 5 requirement in a sensitivity analysis gave medians of 8.4 and 14.6 months (HR 0.63). At this interim analysis, overall survival did not meet its boundary (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.57–1.11, one-sided p=0.087). Grade ≥3 treatment-related events occurred in 71% vs 32% (combination vs control).
39798578.funding: Funded by Merck Sharp and Dohme and Eisai, which had a declared role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation and writing of the report

limitations: Eligibility and TACE practice differ by region and randomisation was not stratified by site or country, which the authors state
Participants were not recruited from some high-incidence regions including Africa
Progression-free survival is a compound endpoint that might be confounded by competing deaths from cirrhosis in this population
Accessibility to the study and its regional variation might have been affected by socioeconomic or cultural factors
A full analysis of liver function is deferred until mature overall survival and subsequent-therapy data are available
critique: The primary comparison was changed by protocol amendment in August 2020, after the Independent Data Monitoring Committee had reviewed safety data and in response to the positive IMbrave150 result, from durvalumab plus placebo to durvalumab plus bevacizumab, so the hypothesis that the trial reports as primary was selected during the trial in the light of external evidence about which arm would show benefit

The interim progression-free survival analysis did not reach significance and the result reported is the final analysis against a threshold of 0.044, so the trial became positive only at its second look

The primary publication withheld the nonsignificant interim overall survival result to preserve masking. The final ESMO GI 2026 conference analysis found median overall survival of 29.9 versus 33.3 months for durvalumab–bevacizumab plus TACE versus TACE (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.87–1.39, P = 0.470). The earlier progression-free survival advantage did not translate into a demonstrated survival benefit.

Durvalumab plus TACE was no better than TACE alone (HR 0.94), so the effect is attributable to bevacizumab, and without a bevacizumab-plus-TACE arm the contribution of the checkpoint inhibitor cannot be separated from that of the anti-VEGF antibody

The time-to-deterioration patient-reported endpoints using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-HCC18 were key secondary endpoints and have not been formally tested under the multiple-testing procedure, so no quality-of-life result is available for a regimen that adds months of infusions to a locoregional treatment

Safety was analysed by treatment received (154 triplet, 232 durvalumab–placebo and 200 placebo), versus 204, 207 and 205 randomly assigned. Thirty-nine triplet-assigned patients who received durvalumab without bevacizumab entered the durvalumab–placebo safety group. The resulting counts of treatment-related deaths (0, 3 and 3) may partly reflect this reclassification.

In the triplet safety group, 4/40 patients with baseline varices (10%) had grade 3–4 oesophageal variceal haemorrhage after starting bevacizumab. None was reported in the other safety groups. Baseline portal hypertension and bleeding risk matter when interpreting this small subgroup.

TACE modality, timing and number of procedures (one to four) were all left to the investigator, and bevacizumab was started only after the last TACE, so the trial tests a sequence rather than a defined regimen and its result cannot be mapped onto a specific protocol

The population spans BCLC A (about a quarter) to BCLC C (about a sixth) with half beyond up-to-7, chosen deliberately for breadth, so there is no stage for which the 15-month progression-free survival figure can be said to apply

PD-L1 status was unknown in 23–26% of each treatment arm. Figure 4 reports progression-free survival in prespecified subgroups. The estimates do not establish a PD-L1 or AFP threshold for selecting patients.

A substantial list of prespecified secondary endpoints is explicitly not reported, including the direct comparison between the two durvalumab arms and progression-free survival after subsequent therapy, which are the analyses that would clarify the contribution of each component
Child-Pugh B7 patients were eligible but made up only 2–3% of each arm. The trial provides little information about benefit or safety in Child-Pugh B.

The funder had a role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation and writing, sponsor statisticians are among the authors and among those who accessed and verified the data, so no analysis independent of AstraZeneca underlies the result
39798579.n: EMERALD-1 randomised 616 of 887 screened patients with unresectable, embolisation-eligible HCC (BCLC A–C) at 157 sites in 18 countries to durvalumab–bevacizumab plus TACE (204), durvalumab–placebo plus TACE (207) or placebo plus TACE (205). About half exceeded up-to-seven criteria and 42/616 (7%) had portal vein macrovascular invasion.
39798579.bottom_line: In EMERALD-1, durvalumab–bevacizumab plus TACE improved median progression-free survival versus TACE control (15.0 versus 8.2 months, HR 0.77). Durvalumab plus TACE alone had HR 0.94. The trial amended its primary comparison to the bevacizumab-containing arm and did not isolate the contribution of each drug. Final overall survival presented at ESMO GI 2026 was 29.9 versus 33.3 months for the triplet versus control (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.87–1.39). These conference results did not show a survival advantage.
39798579.funding: AstraZeneca funded the trial and participated in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation and writing. Sponsor statisticians were authors. Twelve of 26 academic authors reported consultancy or honoraria from AstraZeneca.

limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede only that recurrence-free survival is a composite endpoint combining recurrence, which affects 40% of patients at three years, with death that may follow from cirrhosis or from treatment toxicity; that the initially positive and ultimately negative result may be explained by a lack of proportional hazards; that the episode is 'a cautionary note to assessing data at early interim time points' and underscores the importance of designing an interim analysis robust enough to call a trial positive under conventional stopping rules; that overall survival remained immature with more than 80% of patients alive in both arms at two years; that follow-up is continuing; and that non-proportional hazards in neoadjuvant and adjuvant HCC trials 'will require a thorough analysis' which they do not provide.
critique: AASLD graded the 2023 recommendation for adjuvant treatment as Level 2, strong, and the 2025 recommendation against routine adjuvant treatment as Level 1, strong. The change followed longer follow-up of the same trial, illustrating how an interim recurrence-free survival result can change.

Reference 3, which supports the quoted account of the original positive result, is a Roche press release titled 'Roche's Tecentriq plus Avastin is the first treatment combination to reduce the risk of cancer returning in people with certain types of early-stage liver cancer in a Phase III trial', with no journal, year, date or locator. The update reproduces the 2023 guidance's citation of a company announcement instead of replacing it with the peer-reviewed report, in the document whose purpose is to correct what that announcement supported.

The updated analysis is cited only as Yopp et al., Annals of Oncology 2024;35:S1230, abstract LBA39. A Level 1 Strong recommendation against a whole class of perioperative therapy rests on a one-page conference abstract with no protocol, no analysis plan and no peer review.

The overall survival hazard ratio is 1.26 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.87), a point estimate favouring surveillance over treatment, and the authors print it and then write that recurrence-free and overall survival results were consistent across subgroups. A numerical signal of harm with an interval that excludes nothing clinically important draws no comment at all.

The 2025 update strengthened the 2023 advice against neoadjuvant systemic therapy from Level 2, weak, to Level 1, strong. IMbrave050 tested adjuvant treatment. Neoadjuvant evidence cited included a 15-patient single-arm phase Ib study and a randomised phase 2 comparison of two perioperative immunotherapy regimens in which 20 patients underwent resection. Neither trial compared neoadjuvant therapy with surgery alone.

The second interim analysis is still an interim analysis, at 35.1 months median follow-up with follow-up ongoing. The reversal therefore rests on data of the same kind as the data that produced the original error, and the update does not say what would make it change again or when it will be revisited.

Patients already receiving adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab under the 2023 recommendation are not mentioned. A guidance that created a treatment population withdraws the recommendation without saying whether those patients should stop, complete the eleven-to-twelve-month course, or be managed some other way.

Recurrence after adjuvant therapy is left to the revised Figure 11, which is the generic recurrence algorithm and draws no distinction for patients who have already had a checkpoint inhibitor. Prior exposure bears on salvage transplantation and on first-line systemic choice, and the 2023 document had at least addressed it by expert opinion.

The remedy offered for the methodological failure is a pointer rather than a method. The update cites a triple-negative breast cancer trial that used restricted mean survival time and says the hazards problem will require thorough analysis, but sets no endpoint standard, no alpha-spending requirement and no minimum follow-up for future HCC adjuvant trials, while naming four ongoing phase 3 adjuvant trials that will report under the same conventions.

The update says AASLD 'is considering innovative methods to bring timely updates, such as this one, to the field'. No process, trigger or interval is described, so the mechanism that produced this correction is not one a reader can rely on for the next one.

In the published version preserved text is in quotation marks and altered text is underlined. The underlining is lost in this extracted copy, so which sentences were changed and which were carried across cannot be determined from the text as read here.
39992051.bottom_line: AASLD 2025 advises against adjuvant and neoadjuvant systemic therapy for patients undergoing liver resection or local ablation for HCC outside trials (Level 1, strong). In the updated IMbrave050 analysis, the recurrence-free survival HR was 0.90 (95% CI 0.72–1.12) and the immature overall survival HR was 1.26 (0.85–1.87). The 2023 guidance supported adjuvant therapy (Level 2, strong) and advised against neoadjuvant systemic therapy (Level 2, weak). IMbrave050 addressed only adjuvant treatment.
39992051.funding: No funding statement appears anywhere in the three-page update. Two of the five authors declare conflicts: one consults for Exelixis, Genentech and AstraZeneca, and the senior author consults for Eisai, Merck, Roche, Genentech, AstraZeneca, Bayer, AbbVie, Sanofi, Moderna, Glycotest and Exelixis and sits on a data safety monitoring board for BMS, with all fees paid to his institution; the remaining three report none

limitations: Patients with Vp4 portal vein thrombosis were excluded

Open-label design; the authors state that although overall survival was not biased by the assigned treatment, the determination of adverse-event causality and health-related quality of life might have been influenced by awareness of treatment
The proportional hazards assumption was violated, so the authors report restricted mean survival time, piecewise hazard ratios and a MaxCombo test alongside the overall hazard ratio
The authors state that the cause of the early crossing of the survival curves is probably multifactorial
critique: The early excess of deaths is explained by the authors as an imbalance in deaths attributed to adverse events unrelated to study treatment, as assessed by investigators, so an excess of early deaths in the experimental arm of an open-label trial is set aside on the basis of unblinded causality judgments by the people delivering the treatment

The restricted mean survival time was similar between arms at 26 and 36 months and differs by only 2.8 months (95% CI 0.2 to 5.4) at 47 months, after nearly all follow-up had accrued, and the paper states that the restricted mean timepoints were explored post hoc

The cut-point for the piecewise hazard ratio was chosen by maximising the partial log likelihood over a grid of candidate timepoints, so the 6-month boundary that defines both the early hazard and the later benefit is data-derived rather than prespecified

Two protocol amendments between April 2019 and February 2023 changed the statistical assumptions to preserve power as events accrued, so the design against which the interim analysis was judged was revised during the trial

Objective response was 36% versus 13% for nivolumab–ipilimumab versus a kinase inhibitor. Exploratory median progression-free survival was 9.1 versus 9.2 months (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.72–1.06), with 34% versus 18% progression-free at 18 months and 28% versus 12% at 24 months. Best response was progressive disease in 20% versus 14%. CheckMate 9DW did not establish efficacy for transplant downstaging.

No dose escalation or reduction was permitted for nivolumab or ipilimumab while dose reductions were allowed for lenvatinib and sorafenib, and treatment was capped at 2 years in the immunotherapy arm only, so the two arms were managed under different rules

At cutoff, all 332 treated nivolumab–ipilimumab patients had discontinued. Progression accounted for 40% of discontinuations versus 69% on control. In the immunotherapy arm, 74 stopped for treatment-related adverse events, 33 for unrelated adverse events (32% combined) and 54 at the two-year treatment limit (16%).

Safety was an exploratory endpoint and no grade 5 treatment-related events are tabulated because grade 5 required death within 24 hours of onset; the 12 treatment-related deaths, 11 of them in the first 6 months, appear only in the text

The post hoc comparisons against each comparator separately give hazard ratios of 0.77 against lenvatinib and 0.42 against sorafenib, but only 50 patients received sorafenib, so the more favourable figure rests on a group smaller than most phase 2 trials

Subsequent immunotherapy was more common after lenvatinib or sorafenib (115/333, 35%) than after nivolumab plus ipilimumab (44/335, 13%). This difference could attenuate an overall survival difference between the randomised strategies. The size and direction of its effect cannot be established from these nonrandomised later treatments.

Eligibility excluded Vp4 invasion, significant ascites, grade 2 encephalopathy in the preceding year and prior transplantation, and required Child-Pugh 5 or 6, so the regimen's early hazard was measured in the fittest patients available

The comparator is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor at a time when immunotherapy combinations are first-line, so the trial cannot say whether this regimen should displace atezolizumab plus bevacizumab or durvalumab plus tremelimumab

Bristol Myers Squibb provided trial agents, collaborated on design, data collection, analysis and interpretation, and funded writing support. Five sponsor employees were credited with the data analysis.
40349714.n: 668 patients with unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh 5 or 6, ECOG 0 or 1 and no previous systemic therapy, randomised 1:1 at 163 centres in 25 countries between January 2020 and November 2021 to nivolumab plus ipilimumab (335) or investigator's choice of lenvatinib or sorafenib (333); of the 325 treated controls, 275 (85 percent) received lenvatinib and 50 (15 percent) sorafenib
40349714.bottom_line: First-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab improved median overall survival versus lenvatinib or sorafenib (23.7 versus 20.6 months, HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65–0.96, P = 0.018) and objective response (36% versus 13%). The survival curves crossed. The death HR was 1.65 (1.12–2.43) in the first six months before later separation favoured immunotherapy. Restricted mean survival was 2.8 months longer through 47 months. Exploratory median progression-free survival was similar. The trial did not compare current immunotherapy doublets with one another.
40349714.funding: Bristol Myers Squibb supplied the trial agents, collaborated with academic investigators on trial design, data collection, analysis and interpretation, and funded medical writing, including the first draft. Five sponsor employees were credited with the data analysis.

limitations: About 90 percent of patients had a solitary tumour and more than half a largest diameter of 2 cm or less, so the authors state the result may best apply to a single tumour of 2 cm or less and that applying it to three nodules up to 3 cm would overestimate the findings

Patients whose tumour lay close to vasculature, the biliary tree or adjacent organs, or was poorly seen on ultrasound, were excluded if judged unfeasible for ablation, so the authors advise that ablation in difficult locations and above 2 cm needs careful indication
Because enrolment was discontinued, the analysis does not account for multiplicity across the two co-primary endpoints

SURF tested radiofrequency ablation and included many open resections early in accrual. In discussing transferability, the authors cite meta-analyses comparing open with minimally invasive surgery and randomised trials comparing radiofrequency with microwave ablation. SURF did not directly test either substitution.
The number of patients who had a pretreatment biopsy is unclear, because biopsy was not routine in Japanese practice during the study period
LI-RADS criteria were not used; the authors state that by their own dynamic CT definition about 90 to 95 percent of the surgical patients were correctly diagnosed as HCC
In the observational cohort the groups were imbalanced at baseline, with a largest diameter of 2 cm or less in 50 percent of surgical against 72 percent of ablation patients
critique: The trial was designed to show the superiority of surgery and did not, with 67.2 percent power for a 10-point difference and 80 percent power only for 11.6 points, so this is a failed superiority trial; the Discussion nonetheless closes by asserting the equivalent effectiveness of both treatments

The local recurrence comparison was converted between reports: the same 12 and 24 events were 15.0 and 28.0 percent of patients with recurrence in 2022 (p = 0.07) and are 8.0 and 15.8 percent of all randomised patients here (p = 0.03), so a change of denominator turns a non-significant finding into the significant one the Discussion relies on

The definition of a successful ablation also changed: the 2022 report accepted RECICL TE4a or TE4b, explicitly including complete response without an adequate margin, while this report states success required TE4a with an adequate margin, so the two papers describe the same procedures by different standards

The original and final reports give slightly different flow counts: 1,090 vs 1,094 assessed, 778 vs 782 declining randomisation, seven vs six exclusions after registration and 151 vs 152 eligible for ablation. Losses also rose from 25 to 35 per arm with longer follow-up.

The paper reports Hochberg-adjusted p values of .84 for both co-primary endpoints while the limitations state that multiplicity was not accounted for; the adjustment simply assigns the recurrence endpoint the larger of the pair (unadjusted .50 becoming .84), and the paper contradicts itself about whether any adjustment was made

In the observational cohort the unadjusted recurrence-free survival favoured surgery (HR 0.80, p = .02) and after weighting became HR 0.84 with p = .08, so the headline of no difference rests on a p value crossing 0.05 rather than on the estimate changing, and the weighted curves in Figure 4 are footnoted as carrying unadjusted at-risk numbers

Recurrence was detected by MRI in 17.5 percent of surgical against 31.9 percent of ablation recurrences in the trial, so the arm with more local recurrence was also imaged more sensitively, and this asymmetry (p = .08) is tabulated without comment

Serious adverse effects were collected but post-treatment complications were not, giving 3.3 percent in the surgery arm and zero in 152 ablations, a figure the Discussion does not use but the abstract reports

Equal survival despite doubled local recurrence is achieved by an intensive salvage system: in the cohort, 26.3 percent of surgical recurrences were resected again against 5.2 percent of ablation recurrences, while 68.3 percent of ablation recurrences were re-ablated (p < .01), so the result describes Japanese retreatment capacity as much as the index procedure

The authors use the surgical arm's pathology to claim that 90 to 95 percent of patients were correctly diagnosed, which concedes that 5 to 10 percent of resected patients did not have HCC and leaves no corresponding check available for the ablation arm, where biopsy was rare

The SURF-Cohort consists of the 753 patients who refused randomisation and were treated by clinician preference, and is offered as a way to interpret and extrapolate the trial, when it embodies exactly the selection the trial was meant to remove: the paper's own forest plot shows surgery was chosen for tumours above 2 cm (OR 2.76) and ablation for low platelets and prior chemoembolisation
The study design included 118 institutions. The final report identifies 49 institutions that accrued patients. These figures describe different stages of participation.

Patients who died of other diseases without recurrence were censored rather than counted, in a cirrhotic population in which non-cancer death is a competing risk, and no competing-risk analysis of recurrence is presented
40554738.n: 1,094 patients assessed at 49 of 118 Japanese institutions between April 2009 and August 2015, yielding 302 in the randomised SURF-RCT (surgery 150, ablation 152) and 753 who declined randomisation in the parallel SURF-Cohort (surgery 382, ablation 371); 90 percent of the randomised patients had a solitary tumour with a median diameter of 1.8 cm
40554738.bottom_line: The final SURF report: 5-year overall survival was 74.6 percent after surgery and 70.4 percent after ablation (HR 0.96, adjusted p = 0.84) with recurrence-free survival 42.9 versus 42.7 percent (HR 0.90), and the 753-patient observational cohort agreed after weighting. Local recurrence was twice as common after ablation in both studies, the trial had 67.2 percent power for the 10-point difference it was designed to find, difficult tumour locations were excluded, and several figures including the local-recurrence denominators and the ablation success definition changed between this report and the 2022 one.
40554738.funding: Supported by the Japanese Foundation for Multidisciplinary Treatment of Cancer and Health and Labour Sciences Research Grant for Clinical Cancer Research H21-015; most authors report honoraria, research funding or advisory roles with industry, including Wako Diagnostics, Chugai, Eisai, AstraZeneca, Medtronic and Terumo

limitations: The update identifies unresolved thresholds for resection with portal hypertension, AFP response after downstaging, TACE suitability and major response. It notes immature survival data, under-accrual in some radiotherapy trials, limited portal-vein invasion data and residual confounding in observational comparisons. CUSE has not been shown to improve outcomes. The text describes its online tool in different passages as both developed and under development.
critique: The PubMed search was restricted to human studies in adults aged over 19 and English-language publications. This may limit capture of relevant studies from other languages. The search restrictions alone cannot explain the place assigned to a particular modality.

Two of the three evidence syntheses underpinning the update are the authors' own: an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of external beam radiotherapy in about 5,000 patients and an aggregate-data meta-analysis of 73 studies in macrovascular invasion. The group that sets the algorithm also produced the evidence that moved it, and the update does not treat that as a source of bias.

CUSE structures discussion of complexity, uncertainty, subjectivity and emotion. The guideline describes categories for proceeding, considering or declining an option. Its effect on decisions and outcomes has not been evaluated. The article describes its web tool inconsistently, as developed in one passage and still under development in another.

EBRT and TARE enter the figure for BCLC 0 and A on data the update itself qualifies in the same paragraphs: RASER with a mean tumour size of 2.1 cm and standard deviation 0.4, LEGACY with a median of 2.6 cm and a range to 8.1 cm, and an EBRT literature described as limited by heterogeneity and selection bias with trials that failed to meet accrual. The position changed; the class of evidence did not.

BCLC 2026 prefers microwave up to 3–4 cm on local-control evidence, including Sugimoto 2025 (PMID 39802807), whose single-needle RFA comparison found less lesion-level progression without a demonstrated survival advantage. Earlier negative trials and device/population differences limit a universal preference.

The update refuses to present cross-trial hazard ratios or survival-curve metrics so as not to imply a hierarchy unsupported by direct evidence, then admits four first-line doublets to BCLC C with no means of choosing between them. The refusal is methodologically defensible and leaves the clinician holding the decision the document exists to inform.

BCLC 2026 explains the change in its BCLC D estimate. Those meeting the strict stage definition have median survival under three months. Figure 5 gives under 12 months for the broader supportive-care group, which includes longer survivors, and the update refers readers to supplementary section B.
The BCLC 2026 main text does not set out an adjuvant systemic therapy position. AASLD addresses this question in its 2025 critical update.

Figure 4 argues that progression-free survival is an unreliable surrogate for overall survival because the same interval can be produced by indolent progression, lethal progression, aggressive biology or treatment-related death. The argument is correct, and the update does not apply it to its own reliance on objective response, complete pathological response and local control in the BCLC 0 and A recommendations it has just expanded.

BCLC cites complete pathological response in different selected populations, including 34% versus 20% on explant in an observational TARE–TACE comparison and 25% in an 88-patient SBRT series. It also describes complete necrosis after superselective TACE. The different populations and denominators preclude cross-study ranking. Imaging response and histological necrosis are distinct, and pathological response has not been established as a surrogate for survival here.

The competing-interest record is corrupted in this copy: one author's entry ends 'and grants from;' with no list, another repeats the same company list twice, and a third reads ': ; none'. For a document whose recommendations now favour named devices and agents, the disclosures as published here cannot be read in full.
41151697.bottom_line: BCLC 2026 includes EBRT and radioembolisation among selected early-stage options and discusses microwave ablation for tumours up to 3–4 cm. It defines multifocal disease numerically and includes ECOG 2 and four systemic doublets in BCLC C. Figure 5 gives median survival under 12 months for the broader BCLC D group and under three months for strictly defined BCLC D. The update leaves several choices to multidisciplinary judgement, including resection with portal hypertension, TACE suitability and response sufficient for downstaging.
41151697.funding: No commercial funding for the update; grant support is listed author by author from Instituto de Salud Carlos III, CIBER and CIBEREHD, AECC, World Cancer Research, an EASL registry grant and institutional research support, with several authors reporting none. Industry relationships are printed in full and are extensive, including consultancy, lecture, travel and institutional educational support from AstraZeneca, Bayer, BMS, Roche/Genentech, Eisai, Lilly, Ipsen, Boston Scientific, Sirtex, Terumo, Guerbet and others; one entry reads 'and grants from;' with nothing after it and another repeats an identical company list twice

limitations: Both trials enrolled heterogeneous populations spanning BCLC A to C, which the authors say may limit applicability to a well-defined intermediate-stage population
The authors note that BCLC A patients have a favourable prognosis and that the medicalisation required by these regimens may have conferred undue risk without commensurate benefit
Neither trial addressed whether adding locoregional therapy to systemic therapy improves outcomes, only the reverse
Chemoembolisation modality, technique and selectivity were variably reported in both trials
Delayed initiation of bevacizumab in EMERALD-1 may have blunted its effect
Progression-free survival is not a validated surrogate for overall survival in this setting
Quality-of-life data had not been reported for either trial at the time of writing
critique: The review is an expert narrative with no systematic search, no inclusion criteria and no evidence grading, so its appraisal cannot be separated from the judgment of its four authors

Two of the four authors disclosed financial relationships involving manufacturers of both regimens. A third disclosed relationships with AstraZeneca and device companies. The article prints no disclosure for the fourth author.

The review disclaims cross-trial comparison and then tabulates the two trials side by side, although they differ in eligibility (Child-Pugh B7 and Vp1 to Vp2 invasion allowed in one and excluded in the other), in chemoembolisation schedule and in the sequencing of the systemic agents, so the table invites the comparison the text forbids
For LEAP-012, Table 1 of the review lists RECIST 1.1 response as 47% vs 37%. The primary trial, the review text and Figure 2 support approximately 47% vs 33% (46.8% vs 33.3% in the figure).

For LEAP-012, the review text misprints the combination PFS confidence interval as 12.6–10.0 months. Figure 2A correctly gives 12.6–16.7 months but prints the hazard ratio interval as 0.15–0.84. The primary report gives HR 0.66 (95% CI 0.51–0.84).

The review identifies quality-of-life data as additional support for interpreting a progression-free survival benefit. Those data were unavailable at publication, leaving the patient-reported trade-off with toxicity uncertain.
The alternative it raises, giving the same drugs sequentially after progression rather than concurrently, is never tested against any data, and no trial addressing it is identified
No formal assessment of either trial's risk of bias is attempted, in a review whose central claim is that the trials' endpoints are insufficient
41503570.bottom_line: A narrative review by two interventional radiologists, a hepatologist and a medical oncologist arguing that the progression-free survival gains in LEAP-012 and EMERALD-1 do not yet justify routine adoption of chemoembolisation plus immunotherapy without survival or quality-of-life data. Its most useful observation is that over 40 percent of each trial lay outside intermediate stage and that neither trial had a systemic-therapy-only arm, so the question of whether to add chemoembolisation to systemic therapy remains unasked.
41503570.funding: Funding and disclosures. The first author reported NCI grant R01 CA256977. Singal and Kelley disclosed industry relationships involving manufacturers of both regimens. Garcia-Reyes listed AstraZeneca and several device companies. No disclosure was printed for Kim.

limitations: Open-label design and lack of statistical power for subgroups, carried over from the primary report
The post hoc up-to-7 subgroup analysis was not prespecified and can only be considered hypothesis-generating

The relative risk of recurrence changed over time, so the Cox hazard ratio is an aggregation of time-varying hazards and should be interpreted with caution; the authors suggest restricted mean survival time would be more accurate
The authors state that the imbalance in deaths together with the reduced recurrence-free survival benefit shifts the benefit-risk assessment negative, particularly after curative-intent treatment
The authors state that the updated results do not support use of the regimen in the adjuvant setting and that the effect on late recurrences of different aetiology is unclear
critique: The surveillance arm's median recurrence-free survival (36.0 months) is longer than the treated arm's (33.2 months) and recurrence occurred in 49 percent of each arm, so the stratified hazard ratio of 0.90 is the aggregate of a curve that crosses rather than a residual benefit

The authors discuss whether bevacizumab can temporarily obscure relapse on imaging and whether stopping it might produce more aggressive recurrence. The first hypothesis remained untested and observed recurrence burden and sites did not suggest more aggressive disease. The updated randomised estimate did not support a sustained adjuvant benefit.

The curves separated at 3 months, reached maximum difference at 9 months and intersected at about 2 years, and the hazard-rate analysis places the peak of recurrence at 6 months in the control arm against 18 months in the treated arm, so twelve months of treatment moved recurrence by roughly the duration of treatment

The exploratory recurrence-free survival HR was 1.01 (95% CI 0.70–1.46) within up-to-seven criteria and 0.84 (0.62–1.13) beyond them. The estimates do not establish benefit or harm in either subgroup or justify selection by up-to-seven status.

Ninety-nine surveillance patients (30 percent) crossed over, some after a second resection or ablation, and one surveillance patient was mistakenly treated and counted in the treated safety population, so neither survival arm is a clean comparison

Death was the most frequent reason for leaving study follow-up (54/334, 16%, after atezolizumab–bevacizumab versus 46/334, 14%, with surveillance). The authors identified this imbalance in their unfavourable benefit–risk assessment. The overall survival HR was 1.26 (95% CI 0.85–1.87) and remained immature.

Immune-mediated adverse events occurred in 208 of 332 treated patients (63 percent) against 59 of 330 (18 percent), with 9 percent needing systemic corticosteroids, all in patients who had been rendered disease-free

Screening excluded 57 of 914 assessed patients for residual, recurrent or metastatic disease and 26 for lack of signed consent. These were screen failures. The protocol counted baseline disease detected later by independent review as recurrence at randomisation.

The analysis is descriptive by design because the interim was declared positive, so the trial that changed guidance can no longer be tested on the endpoint that changed it, and the authors recommend for future trials the longer follow-up and non-proportional-hazards methods their own design lacked
Restricted mean survival time is proposed in the limitations as the more accurate measure of effect but no restricted mean survival time estimate is reported anywhere in this paper

Five authors disclosed employment and stock in Roche or Genentech. The sponsor funded medical writing. The figure recapitulating the interim analysis was adapted from Qin and colleagues’ original peer-reviewed Lancet trial report.
41580093.n: The same 668 randomised IMbrave050 patients reanalysed at a 3 May 2024 cutoff with a median follow-up of 35.1 months and a minimum of 29.2 months; 99 of 334 surveillance patients (30 percent) had crossed over to atezolizumab plus bevacizumab
41580093.bottom_line: The descriptive final analysis of IMbrave050 shows the interim recurrence-free survival benefit was not sustained: median recurrence-free survival 33.2 months with treatment against 36.0 months with surveillance, stratified HR 0.90 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.12), recurrence in 162 of 334 against 164 of 334, and overall survival numerically worse (HR 1.26, 0.85 to 1.87). One year of adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab deferred early recurrence without preventing it, at the cost of 63 percent immune-mediated events and an excess of deaths.

limitations: Retrospective design with non-random treatment assignment, which the authors state
Institutional heterogeneity in protocols and supportive care
BCLC misclassification between investigator-reported and adjudicated stage, since staging was re-adjudicated from component variables because reported staging was discordant and often missing

Formal violation of the proportional hazards assumption for several covariates in all four models, so the authors say their hazard ratios should be interpreted with caution and report 3-year restricted mean survival time instead
Confounding of the proton versus photon comparison by geography, access and insurance, which the authors acknowledge
The authors concede that advanced-stage patients included were those most suitable for radiotherapy, with liver-dominant disease
critique: The conclusion that radiotherapy survival is comparable with resection, thermal ablation and other ablative locoregional therapies rests on a comparison with guideline expectations rather than on any measured difference, because the dataset contains no resection, ablation or chemoembolisation arm

Thirty of 96 eligible centres supplied data. Eligibility required published ablative-technique series reporting survival. Selective publication and participation could influence survival estimates, but neither the direction nor the size of that effect is known.

Treatment-naïve BCLC B patients (n = 89) had a median survival of 6.3 years (95% CI 3.9 to not reached), versus 5.4 years for treatment-naïve BCLC A patients. Three-year restricted mean survival was the same. This selected, small subgroup does not recalibrate survival for BCLC B generally.

Re-adjudicating every patient with an ECOG score above 0 into BCLC C may have moved merely comorbid or cirrhotic patients out of the early-stage groups and so inflated early-stage survival, which the authors note but do not quantify

The photon–proton comparison was exploratory. Dose was not a required submission, although Table 2 describes available doses. Incomplete tumour volume, dose, fractionation and planning data limit interpretation of differences between modalities.
Treatment spans 2000 to 2024, pooling planning, immobilisation, image guidance and motion management technologies that differ by a generation, with year of treatment entered only as a covariate
Sixty percent of patients had received prior treatment of any kind, including 58% with prior locoregional therapy. Outcomes for the whole cohort therefore mix first and later lines of EBRT.

Table 4 in the published text contains corrupted confidence intervals (a hazard ratio of 0.82 with an interval of 0.72 to 0.03 and one of 1.60 with an interval of 1.41 to 1.28), and Table 2's modality proportions disagree with the narrative, so the paper's own numbers cannot all be read as printed

The journal’s relevance note, like the authors’ conclusion, presents EBRT as a first-line option to consider. Comparative efficacy against other first-line treatments requires a study with a treatment comparator.
42139645.n: The individual-patient meta-analysis included 4,913 HCC patients treated with ablative EBRT at 30 of 96 eligible centres in 11 countries identified through a systematic review to 15 December 2022. Sixty percent had any previous therapy and 58% had previous locoregional therapy. There was no non-EBRT comparator.
42139645.bottom_line: This pooled individual-patient study reports survival after ablative EBRT by adjudicated BCLC stage. Thirty of 96 eligible centres participated. Eligibility required a published ablative radiotherapy series reporting survival. Sixty percent had received previous therapy, including 58% who had locoregional therapy. All four Cox models violated proportional hazards. Without a concurrent comparison, these data cannot establish equivalence to surgery or ablation.

limitations: No limitations section; the faculty concede only that recommendations from earlier conferences not specifically revised here remain valid, including the whole of HVPG measurement methodology, that the criteria for diagnosing clinically significant portal hypertension carry 'individual limitations' which statement 1.16 asks the clinician to consider without naming them, that non-invasive tests for clinically significant portal hypertension and high-risk varices may not be applicable where there is macrovascular invasion (1.21, LoE 3, weak), that patients in the indeterminate range are handled by re-evaluation at 12 months on LoE 4 weak evidence, and that 153 topics remain open on the research agenda, among them the incidence of and value of six-monthly surveillance for HCC in Budd-Chiari syndrome and whether Milan and AFP-based listing criteria apply in that setting.
critique: The reference list contains seven items, all of them previous Baveno conference reports published between 1992 and 2022. Two hundred and seventy-two statements carry a graded level of evidence, the three new HCC statements among them at LoE 3, with no citation to a single primary study, so no grade in this document can be traced to the evidence that produced it.
The journal reports conference funding and individual faculty relationships on pp. 1014–1015. These disclosures matter when interpreting device-specific elastography cutoffs.
Individual disclosures and links to the ICMJE forms appear on pp. 1014–1015.

Only statements reaching the threshold are published, and the document says so. Nothing shows how many statements were voted on, which failed, or how the agreement figures were distributed, so a reader cannot separate a settled position from a contested one that was dropped; the printed agreement figures run from 80% to 100% and those at the bottom of that range are indistinguishable from statements that never appeared.

Strong consensus is defined as above 80% faculty agreement. Four in five is a low bar for a document that presents itself as consensus, and it means a statement opposed by up to one voting expert in five is printed without that dissent being visible anywhere.

The three HCC statements are all new, LoE 3 and weak, yet written as operational rules. Statement 1.22 extends the rule-out of clinically significant portal hypertension across BCLC stages 0 to C and licenses omitting endoscopy; 1.23 restricts the ANTICIPATE route to BCLC 0 to A 'without large (>5cm) nodules in the right liver lobe'. The 5 cm figure and the right-lobe restriction are stated with no derivation, so the reader cannot tell whether they come from data, from an argument about hepatic vein compression, or from the discussion in the room.

Statement 1.21 withdraws the non-invasive tests exactly where an HCC board needs them, saying they may not be applicable when there is macrovascular invasion, and offers no alternative. The patient in whom portal pressure matters most is returned to unguided judgement, and the retained Baveno VII statement linking clinically significant portal hypertension to decompensation and mortality after resection for HCC still names no threshold at which resection should be declined.

Baveno VIII carries forward the association between clinically significant portal hypertension and outcomes after HCC resection, along with earlier HVPG methodology. It favours noninvasive testing over routine invasive measurement in daily clinical practice. A noninvasive estimate should be interpreted within its validated population.
Statement 1.16 specifies a 100-Hz spleen measurement and restricts the liver-stiffness rule-in to viral or alcohol-related disease and non-obese MASLD (p. 995).
Baveno VIII was published in J Hepatol 85, pp. 993–1018. See pp. 995–996 for the portal-hypertension criteria and pp. 1014–1015 for disclosures.

The paediatric statements are new and were voted by the same faculty, with paediatric hepatologists added to only some panels and the composition of the vote for each statement not reported. The paediatric symposium held alongside the conference was sponsored by a single children's hospital, and the research agenda concedes that paediatric cut-offs for varices still need validation.
On p. 995, statement 1.16c uses >55 kPa for spleen stiffness at 100 Hz. Figure 1 shows ≥55 kPa. The roadmap uses the written statement.
42624290.bottom_line: Establishes the current consensus thresholds for ruling clinically significant portal hypertension in and out without catheterisation, extends them for the first time to patients with HCC across BCLC stages 0 to C, and tells a tumour board that endoscopy may be omitted when liver stiffness is 15 kPa or less with platelets of 150 x 10^9/L or more. It does not establish any of this as validated practice: the three HCC statements are new, LoE 3 and weak, the 5 cm right-lobe caveat is unexplained, the tests are withdrawn where there is macrovascular invasion, and the whole document carries seven references, all to earlier Baveno meetings, so no statement can be checked against the evidence behind it. Take the numbers as the field's working agreement, not as a tested rule.
42624290.funding: The faculty report conference funding from industry partners and individual competing interests, including relationships with elastography manufacturers (pp. 1014–1015).

limitations: Over-representation of participants from Asia, which the authors concede
Open-label design, although the study was sponsor-blinded with centralised randomisation and blinded central review of the primary endpoint

Heterogeneity in treatment practices and investigator-driven post-randomisation decisions around progression, including repeat chemoembolisation and subsequent anticancer therapy, which the authors say could influence outcomes
Findings concern chemoembolisation only, so combinations with transarterial radioembolisation remain unstudied
The cause of a small number of deaths could not be established and remained classified as unknown
The authors note frequent lenvatinib dose modification and discontinuation for adverse events as a reflection of the tolerability burden
critique: Randomisation changed from three arms to two. The 175 people assigned STRIDE plus TACE were compared with the first 175 people concurrently assigned TACE alone. The doublet comparison remains pending in the testing hierarchy because the triplet’s interim overall survival comparison did not cross its prespecified boundary.

At 40% maturity, the interim overall survival HR for triplet versus TACE was 0.84 (95% CI 0.65–1.09). The restricted mean survival difference was 1.48 months (95% CI −1.21 to 4.16). The interim analysis was inconclusive. Final overall survival remains pending.

Subsequent systemic therapy was more common with TACE alone (154/292, 53%) than after the triplet (85/293, 29%). This imbalance could reduce a survival difference between the assigned strategies, although treatment after discontinuation was not randomised and its contribution cannot be quantified.

In the exploratory comparison of concurrent STRIDE–lenvatinib–TACE and STRIDE–TACE groups, response was 39% versus 41% (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.60–1.43) and disease control was 81% versus 74%. Toxicity was greater with lenvatinib. The comparison did not establish its incremental efficacy.

Grade 3 to 4 treatment-related events occurred in 63 against 19 percent, serious adverse events in 64 against 23 percent, and there were seven treatment-related deaths including two from myocarditis, in a population still eligible for embolisation
PD-L1 status is missing in about 80 percent of participants, so the only candidate biomarker is unavailable in four patients out of five

Repeat chemoembolisation and post-progression therapy were at investigator discretion in an open-label trial, and 55 percent of procedures were conventional against 42 percent drug-eluting bead, so neither the control intervention nor the post-progression pathway is standardised

Among 287 patients who received STRIDE–lenvatinib plus TACE, the abstract reports grade 3–4 hypertension of any cause in 34 (12%). The Results text reports treatment-related grade 3–4 hypertension in 29 (10%). The two figures use different attribution rules.

Two separate data cutoffs are reported in one paper, progression-free survival on 2 September 2025 and overall survival on 23 February 2026, with a third cutoff still to come, so the efficacy and survival results describe different datasets
The publisher posted a corrected version on 28 September 2026. The notice in the article does not identify which items changed.
There is no arm receiving the systemic regimen without chemoembolisation, so the incremental value of the embolisation itself in a patient who could have systemic therapy alone is not addressed
AstraZeneca funded the trial, several authors are its employees, and sponsor staff are among those who accessed and verified the data
42636832.n: EMERALD-3 randomised 760 of 1,124 screened Child-Pugh A patients with HCC suitable for TACE but unsuitable for resection, ablation or transplantation at 177 sites in 21 countries. The groups were STRIDE–lenvatinib plus TACE (293), STRIDE plus TACE (175) and TACE alone (292). Overall 62% exceeded up-to-seven criteria, about 10% had Vp1–2 invasion and 72% were Asian.
42636832.bottom_line: Adding STRIDE and lenvatinib to TACE prolonged progression-free survival. At 40% overall survival maturity, the survival HR was 0.84 (95% CI 0.65–1.09, P = 0.18), short of the prespecified P = 0.021 threshold. The final analysis is pending. The STRIDE–TACE doublet was compared with 175 concurrent controls and awaits formal hierarchical testing. Grade 3–4 treatment-related events were 63% versus 19% for triplet versus TACE, with seven treatment-related deaths in the triplet group.
